context: According to Table 1, catalase activity was greatest at which temperature?

why.B: 8.1 mL/min, below the maximum.

why.D: Activity is 0.0 mL/min at this temperature.

context: Based on Table 2, as pH increased from 3.0 to 7.0, catalase activity:

why.A: Correct — values rise steadily from 0.4 to 14.6 across that range.
why.B: The decline occurs only above pH 7.0.
why.C: The reversal happens outside the stated range.
why.D: The values change substantially.

context: Based on Table 1, catalase activity at 30°C would most likely be closest to:

why.A: Below the value already measured at 25°C (8.1).
why.B: Correct — 30°C lies between 25°C (8.1) and 37°C (14.6), so the value must fall between them.
why.C: Exceeds the maximum measured at the optimum.

why.A: Correct — lower pH values indicate greater acidity.
why.B: pH 7.0 is neutral, the dividing line between acidic and basic rather than an acidic value.

context: A sample of catalase is heated to 70°C and then cooled to 37°C. Based on the passage, the activity at 37°C after cooling would most likely be:

choices.text: 14.6 mL/min, the same as before heating.
near 0 mL/min, because the enzyme was permanently altered.
higher than 14.6 mL/min, because heating increases reaction rate.
about half of 14.6 mL/min, because some of the enzyme survives.

why.A: The note states the shape change does not reverse on cooling.
why.B: Correct — above 60°C the enzyme permanently loses its shape and activity does not return.
why.C: The passage shows activity falling, not rising, above the optimum.
why.D: No data support a partial loss; the note says the change above 60°C is permanent for the enzyme.

context: Which of the following pairs of conditions would be expected to produce the lowest catalase activity?

why.A: This is the optimum for both variables.
why.B: Both values are moderately favorable.
why.C: Correct — both conditions are at the extremes where activity approaches zero in each study.
why.D: Both values are somewhat past the optimum but still support meaningful activity.

context: A student claims that catalase activity depends only on temperature. Do the data support this claim?

choices.text: Yes, because activity peaked at 37°C in Study 1.
Yes, because pH was held constant throughout Study 1.
No, because Study 2 shows activity varying substantially at a single constant temperature.
No, because Study 1 used only seven temperatures, which is too few to establish a dependence.

why.A: A temperature optimum does not rule out other factors.
why.B: Holding pH constant in one study says nothing about whether pH matters.
why.C: Correct — at a fixed 37°C, activity ranged from 0.2 to 14.6 mL/min as pH changed.
why.D: The number of temperatures tested is not the reason the claim fails.

context: According to Table 1, Species B germinated best at a soil moisture of:

why.A: Only 48 seeds germinated.
why.B: 76 seeds, below the maximum.
why.C: Correct — 88 seeds germinated, the highest value for Species B.
why.D: Only 29 seeds, the lowest for that species above 10%.

why.A: Correct — values rise from 52 to 88 to 94.
why.B: That describes Species B over the same range.
why.C: No reversal occurs for Species C in this range.
why.D: The values change by 42 seeds.

why.A: Species A peaks at 40% and declines by 50%, so it is past its optimum at 45%.
why.B: Species B declines sharply above 30%, reaching only 29 germinations at 50%.
why.C: Correct — Species C rises continuously through 50%, so at 45% it is near its best for both germination and height.
why.D: The three species respond very differently to moisture.

why.A: At 10% the three species spread only 48 − 5 = 43 seeds, less than the spread at 50%.

why.C: At 30% the three counts sit closest together, spreading only 88 − 52 = 36 seeds.

context: To test whether light exposure affects germination in Species A, the researchers should conduct a trial in which:

choices.text: light is varied while moisture, species, and all other conditions are held constant.
both light and moisture are varied together for all three species.
Species A is grown in complete darkness at a new temperature.
Species B and C are each grown under a different light condition from the one used before.

why.A: Correct — isolating one variable requires changing only that variable.
why.B: Changing two variables makes the result uninterpretable.
why.C: Changing temperature as well confounds the light effect.
why.D: The question concerns Species A specifically.

context: In Experiment 1, which solution produced the greatest mass loss?

why.A: 18 mg, well below the salt solution.
why.B: Correct — 47 mg, the highest value in Experiment 1.
why.C: Only 2 mg, since oxygen was removed.
why.D: Only 1 mg, since water was absent.

context: Trials 3 and 4 were most likely included in order to:

choices.text: test whether temperature changes the rate of corrosion.
confirm that both oxygen and water are required for corrosion.
compare how well two different coatings protect the nails.
measure the density of each of the solutions used.

why.A: Temperature was constant at 20°C throughout Experiment 1.
why.B: Correct — Trial 3 removes oxygen and Trial 4 removes water; both nearly eliminate mass loss.
why.C: Coatings appear only in Experiment 2.
why.D: Density was never measured.

context: Based on Experiment 2, which coating provided the greatest protection?

why.A: Reduced loss to 12 mg, but zinc did better.
why.B: Correct — zinc reduced mass loss to 3 mg, the lowest value.
why.C: Copper increased mass loss to 61 mg, worse than no coating.
why.D: The uncoated control lost 47 mg.

context: The result for the copper-coated nail (Trial 8) is notable because it suggests that:

choices.text: copper prevents water from reaching the iron.
some coatings can accelerate rather than slow corrosion.
copper is chemically identical to zinc.
the experiment was performed at the wrong temperature.

why.A: If it did, mass loss would have decreased, not increased.
why.B: Correct — 61 mg exceeds the uncoated control’s 47 mg.
why.C: The two coatings produced opposite effects.
why.D: All Experiment 2 trials used the same 20°C.

context: Based on Experiment 3, mass lost at 45°C would most likely be closest to:

why.A: Below the value already recorded at 35°C.
why.B: 70 mg is lower than the 78 mg already recorded at 35 °C, and mass lost rises with temperature, so 45 °C cannot come in under it.
why.C: Correct — 45°C lies between 35°C (78) and 50°C (112), so the value must fall between them.
why.D: Exceeds the highest measured value.

context: To determine whether zinc coating remains protective in hot salt water, the next trial should use:

choices.text: a zinc-coated nail in 0.5 M NaCl at 50°C.
an oil-coated nail in distilled water at 50°C.
a zinc-coated nail in distilled water at 20°C.
an uncoated nail in 0.5 M NaCl at 50°C.

why.A: Correct — it holds the coating and solution from Trial 7 and changes only temperature, matching the Experiment 3 condition.
why.B: Changes both coating and solution.
why.C: Changes the solution rather than the temperature.
why.D: Removes the zinc coating, which is the variable of interest.

context: Across all three experiments, which factor was held constant in Experiments 1 and 2 but varied in Experiment 3?

why.A: Solution varied in Experiment 1 and was constant in Experiment 3.
why.B: Coating varied in Experiment 2.
why.C: Correct — 20°C in Experiments 1 and 2; Experiment 3 tested 5, 20, 35, and 50°C.
why.D: Identical iron nails were used throughout.

context: In Experiment 1, which light color produced the least dry mass, excluding the control?

why.A: 1.84 g, well above green.
why.B: Correct — 0.71 g, the lowest value among the illuminated groups.
why.C: Red produced 2.05 g, nearly three times the mass of the lowest illuminated group.
why.D: White light gave 2.31 g, the highest of the illuminated groups rather than the lowest.

context: Group 5 (darkness) was included in Experiment 1 primarily to:

choices.text: test whether the seedlings can survive without any water at all.
serve as a control establishing growth in the absence of light.
measure leaf area more precisely than the method in Experiment 1 allowed.
compare the effects of blue and of red light directly.

why.A: Water was not a variable in this study.
why.B: Correct — a group receiving none of the treatment provides a baseline for comparison.
why.C: Leaf area was measured for all groups alike.
why.D: That comparison uses Groups 1 and 3.

context: Based on Experiment 2, increasing red light intensity from 400 to 800 μmol/m²/s produced:

choices.text: a large increase in dry mass.
a small increase in dry mass.
a large decrease in dry mass.

why.A: The change from 2.44 to 2.49 g is only 0.05 g.
why.B: Correct — dry mass rose slightly, indicating the response is leveling off.
why.C: Mass increased rather than decreased.
why.D: There was a small but nonzero change.

context: Which conclusion is best supported by comparing Experiments 1 and 3?

choices.text: Blue light alone produces more growth than any combination of colors at the same intensity.
A mixture of blue and red light outperforms either color alone at the same intensity.
Green light is essential for reaching maximum growth.
Light intensity has no effect on final dry mass.

why.A: Blue alone gives 1.84 g, the lowest value in Experiment 3.
why.B: Correct — the 25:75 mix produced 2.38 g, exceeding blue alone (1.84) and red alone (2.05).
why.C: Green produced the least growth of any illuminated group.
why.D: Experiment 2 shows a clear intensity effect.

context: In Experiment 1, dry mass and leaf area were related in what way?

choices.text: Groups with greater dry mass generally had greater leaf area.
Groups with greater dry mass generally had smaller leaf area.
Leaf area was identical across all groups.

why.A: Correct — the ranking of dry mass (white > red > blue > green > dark) matches the ranking of leaf area exactly.
why.B: The relationship is direct, not inverse.
why.C: The two rankings align perfectly across all five groups.
why.D: Leaf area ranged from 3 to 81 cm².

context: The relatively poor growth under green light is best explained by the fact that chlorophyll:

choices.text: absorbs green light more strongly than blue or red light.
reflects and transmits green light rather than absorbing it.

why.A: The passage states absorption is strongest in blue and red.
why.B: Correct — plants appear green precisely because chlorophyll reflects green light, so less energy is captured.
why.C: No destruction is described or implied.
why.D: The darkness control shows almost no growth.

context: A grower wants maximum dry mass while minimizing electricity use. Based on all three experiments, the best strategy is to use:

choices.text: 800 μmol/m²/s of red light, the brightest tested.
200 μmol/m²/s of 25:75 blue and red light.

why.A: Yields 2.49 g but at four times the intensity, and the gain over 400 is negligible.
why.B: Correct — 2.38 g at only 200 μmol/m²/s, nearly matching the highest yields at a quarter of the energy.
why.C: Green light produced the poorest illuminated growth.
why.D: At 50 μmol/m²/s the yield is only 0.88 g — cheap to run, but nowhere near maximum dry mass.

context: According to Scientist 1, the timing of the extinctions corresponds most closely to:

choices.text: the timing of global temperature minima.
the arrival of modern humans on each landmass.
the fragmentation of the mammoth steppe.
changes in the pollen records of each region.

why.A: Scientist 1 explicitly rejects a global climate event as the trigger.
why.B: Correct — Scientist 1 cites Australia at 45,000 and North America at 13,000 years ago, each following human arrival.
why.C: That is Scientist 2’s mechanism.
why.D: Pollen evidence is offered by Scientist 2.

context: Scientist 2 cites the small number of confirmed kill sites in order to argue that:

choices.text: humans reached North America later than once believed.
hunting was too limited in scale.
megafauna were already extinct before humans arrived.
archaeological methods are unreliable in this period.

why.A: Arrival timing is not disputed by Scientist 2.
why.B: Correct — "far too few to account for continent-wide extinction."
why.C: Scientist 2 states several species survived alongside humans for millennia.
why.D: Method reliability is never questioned.

context: Both scientists would most likely agree that:

choices.text: human hunting was the primary cause of the extinctions on every landmass where large mammals disappeared.
most large land mammals in several regions of the world went extinct during the late Pleistocene.
climate change had no role at all in the late Pleistocene extinctions.
Africa lost most of its megafauna along with the other continents.

why.A: Scientist 2 rejects this.
why.B: Correct — the shared premise is stated in the introduction and accepted by both.
why.C: Scientist 2 makes climate the central cause.
why.D: Scientist 1 notes Africa retained most of its large mammals.

context: Which finding, if true, would most weaken Scientist 2’s hypothesis?

choices.text: Pollen shows vegetation changing 2,000 years before the extinctions everywhere.
Island species died out where vegetation was unchanged.
Mammoth steppe habitat declined sharply everywhere after 15,000 years ago.
Fewer than 20 confirmed kill sites exist anywhere in North America.

why.A: This supports Scientist 2 by placing habitat change before the losses.
why.B: Correct — extinction without habitat change breaks the causal link Scientist 2 proposes.
why.C: This is precisely Scientist 2’s claim.
why.D: This is evidence Scientist 2 already cites in support.

context: Scientist 1 uses the case of Africa to argue that:

choices.text: African climate was considerably more stable than the climate elsewhere.
prey species that had coevolved with hominins were less vulnerable to human hunting.
African megafauna were smaller and reproduced faster than the megafauna of other continents.
humans in Africa never hunted large mammals of any size.

why.A: Scientist 1 does not appeal to African climate.
why.B: Correct — "precisely what one would expect if naive prey animals were the vulnerable ones."
why.C: Body size and reproduction in Africa are not discussed.
why.D: Scientist 1 implies long coexistence, not an absence of hunting.

context: Scientist 1 argues that extinction could result from a modest hunting rate because large mammals:

choices.text: migrate over long distances between summer and winter ranges each year.
reproduce slowly, so small increases in mortality accumulate.
depend entirely on a grassland habitat that was already disappearing.
have no natural predators other than humans.

why.A: Migration is not part of the argument.
why.B: Correct — "Large, slow-reproducing species need only a small sustained increase in mortality to decline."
why.C: Habitat dependence is Scientist 2’s emphasis.
why.D: Predation by non-humans is never mentioned.

context: Evidence that megafauna in Eurasia declined gradually over 10,000 years of human coexistence would:

choices.text: support Scientist 1 and weaken Scientist 2 in equal measure.
support Scientist 2, who cites long coexistence with humans as evidence against overkill.
support neither, because Eurasia lies outside both hypotheses.
prove that no climate change occurred at the glacial period’s end.

why.A: Scientist 1’s model emphasizes losses shortly after human arrival.
why.B: Correct — Scientist 2 argues that species surviving for millennia alongside humans is inconsistent with a rapid, hunting-driven collapse.
why.C: It bears directly on the dispute: Scientist 2 treats survival for millennia alongside humans, on any landmass, as evidence against overkill.
why.D: It says nothing about whether climate changed.

No, because KNO₃ is the most soluble at 20°C but not the densest.

why.B: KNO₃ is second in solubility at 20°C, not first.

choices.text: Yes — material produced a 37°C spread, room temperature only 15°C.

choices.text: absorb sunlight more efficiently than shallow roots.
reduce the tree’s need for carbon dioxide.
increase the rate of photosynthesis directly.

context: A student concludes that rainfall is the only factor controlling oak ring width. The data:

choices.text: support this, since oak width rises and falls with rainfall.

refute this, because oak width is unrelated to rainfall.

why.C: Oak width clearly tracks rainfall.
why.D: Juniper shows almost no response, not the same pattern.

context: Experiment 2 shows that the period of a pendulum is:

choices.text: inversely proportional to the mass of the bob.
dependent on both mass and length equally.

why.A: A tenfold mass increase changed the period by at most 0.01 s.
why.B: Correct — the period stayed at about 2.01 s across all masses.
why.C: The period did not fall as mass rose.
why.D: Length clearly matters; mass clearly does not.

context: Based on Experiment 1, a 125 cm string would give a period closest to:

why.A: Below the 100 cm value of 2.01 s.
why.B: Correct — 125 cm lies between 100 cm (2.01 s) and 150 cm (2.46 s).
why.C: 2.60 s exceeds the 2.46 s measured at 150 cm, so it is too long for a 125 cm string.
why.D: Far beyond any measured value.

context: Which variable was held constant in all three experiments?

why.A: Length varied in Experiment 1.
why.B: Mass varied in Experiment 2.
why.C: Angle varied in Experiment 3.
why.D: Correct — each of the three was the independent variable in one experiment.

context: Experiment 3 suggests that release angle:

choices.text: has no effect on the period at any angle tested.
matters at large angles, not small ones.
has a large effect at every one of the angles tested.
decreases the period steadily as the angle increases.

why.A: The period rose from 2.00 to 2.18 s between 5° and 45°.
why.B: Correct — 5° to 10° changed it by 0.01 s, while 20° to 45° changed it by 0.14 s.
why.C: The effect is negligible below 20°.
why.D: The period increased rather than decreased.

context: A student wants a pendulum with a period of exactly 1.00 s. Based on the data, they should use a string of:

choices.text: 25 cm, with any mass and a small release angle
50 cm, with any mass and a small release angle
100 cm, with a light bob and a small release angle
25 cm, but only with a bob of 100 g or less

why.A: Correct — Trial 1 gives 1.00 s at 25 cm, and Experiment 2 shows mass is irrelevant.
why.B: At 50 cm the period is about 1.42 s, so the length is wrong no matter what the bob weighs.
why.C: At 100 cm the period is about 2.01 s; a lighter bob does not shorten it, since mass has no effect.
why.D: The mass restriction is unnecessary, since mass does not affect the period.

context: Quadrupling the string length from 25 cm to 100 cm changed the period by a factor closest to:

why.A: The period clearly changed.
why.B: Correct — 2.01 ÷ 1.00 ≈ 2, so quadrupling the length doubles the period.
why.C: That would require a period of about 4 s.
why.D: Far beyond the observed change.

context: Why did the students time 20 swings and then divide, rather than timing one swing?

choices.text: To reduce the effect of reaction-time error on each measurement of the period.
Because a single swing cannot be timed accurately with a hand stopwatch at all.
To increase the pendulum’s measured period.
To change the release angle between trials.

why.A: Correct — spreading a fixed timing error across 20 swings reduces its effect on the calculated period by a factor of 20.
why.B: A single swing can be timed, just less precisely.
why.C: The method does not alter the pendulum’s behavior.
why.D: Angle was controlled separately.

context: According to Scientist 1, the cooling was triggered by:

choices.text: soot thrown up by continental wildfires.

why.A: That is Scientist 2’s mechanism.
why.B: Correct — meltwater lowered salinity and weakened the northward heat transport.
why.C: Volcanism is never mentioned.
why.D: Orbital change is not discussed by either scientist.

context: Scientist 2 cites platinum, microspherules, and nanodiamonds primarily to argue that:

choices.text: the cooling lasted for roughly 1,200 years before reversing.
an extraterrestrial impact occurred at that time.
ocean circulation weakened in the North Atlantic.
glacial lakes drained rapidly into the North Atlantic.

why.A: Duration is stated in the introduction and is not what these materials show.
why.B: Correct — Scientist 2 links these materials to impacts and notes lake drainage cannot produce them.
why.C: That is Scientist 1’s mechanism.
why.D: Scientist 2 argues against drainage as the cause.

context: Both scientists would most likely agree that:

choices.text: a comet fragmented over the North American ice sheet 12,900 years ago.
the Northern Hemisphere cooled abruptly about 12,900 years ago and stayed cold for centuries.
ocean circulation was unaffected throughout the cooling.
the cooling came on gradually rather than abruptly.

why.A: Only Scientist 2 makes this claim.
why.B: Correct — the shared premise is stated in the introduction and accepted by both.
why.C: Scientist 1 makes circulation central.
why.D: Both describe an abrupt onset.

context: Which finding would most weaken Scientist 1’s hypothesis?

choices.text: Evidence that the Southern Hemisphere cooled just as much as the Northern.
Evidence of elevated platinum in sediments at many sites.
Evidence that the cooling began within a few decades.
Evidence that a large glacial lake existed in North America at exactly that time.

why.A: Correct — Scientist 1’s mechanism predicts an asymmetric, northern-focused cooling, so symmetric cooling contradicts it directly.
why.B: This supports Scientist 2 without disproving a circulation change.
why.C: Scientist 2 emphasizes abruptness, but a sudden lake drainage could also act quickly.
why.D: This supports Scientist 1.

context: Scientist 1 cites St. Lawrence sediment cores in order to:

choices.text: date the impact layer at the St. Lawrence outlet.
provide physical evidence that a large discharge occurred at the right time.
measure Southern Hemisphere temperatures during the 1,200 years the cooling lasted.
show that continent-scale wildfires were widespread.

why.A: Scientist 1 rejects the impact explanation.
why.B: Correct — the cores document the drainage event the hypothesis requires.
why.C: The cores are from North America, not the Southern Hemisphere.
why.D: Wildfires belong to Scientist 2’s account.

context: Scientist 2 argues the abruptness of the onset favors an impact because:

choices.text: oceanographic changes are always slow and could never act within decades.
a sudden catastrophic trigger better matches a change that arrives within a few decades.
impacts always cause cooling wherever they occur.
ice cores cannot resolve intervals as short as decades, so the timing is uncertain.

why.A: Scientist 2 says a catastrophic trigger fits better, not that ocean change is always slow.
why.B: Correct — this is the stated reasoning about timescale.
why.C: No such universal claim is made.
why.D: Scientist 2 relies on decadal resolution rather than disputing it.

context: If the impact materials were later shown to occur at many different dates rather than only at 12,900 years ago, this would:

choices.text: weaken Scientist 2 by cutting the link.
weaken Scientist 1’s hypothesis instead of the other.
have no bearing on either hypothesis, since neither depends on the impact materials.

why.A: The argument depends on the materials being confined to that layer.
why.B: Correct — if the markers are common across many dates, they no longer single out the Younger Dryas onset.
why.C: Scientist 1’s meltwater mechanism is untouched by this finding.
why.D: It bears directly on Scientist 2’s central evidence.

context: The two hypotheses differ mainly in:

choices.text: whether the cooling occurred at all.
the mechanism that initiated the cooling.

why.A: Both accept the cooling as established.
why.B: Correct — meltwater disrupting circulation versus an impact triggering wildfires and soot.
why.C: Neither disputes the roughly 1,200-year duration.
why.D: Only Scientist 1 raises hemispheric asymmetry, and Scientist 2 does not contest it.

context: According to Figure 1, the absorbance of the sample exposed at 800 lux first fell below 0.20 between:

why.C: On the 800 lux curve the reading at 30 minutes is 0.31, which is above 0.20, and the reading at 45 minutes is 0.17, which is below it. The crossing therefore happens between 30 and 45 minutes.
why.A: Covers the steepest part of the curve, but absorbance is still 0.55 at 15 minutes.
why.B: Ends at 0.31, which has not yet fallen below the threshold.
why.D: Begins at 0.17, by which point the curve has already crossed.

context: All samples in both studies were held at 22 degrees C in a water bath. The most likely reason for this choice was to:

choices.text: ensure any difference in fading was due to light rather than temperature.
raise the temperature enough that the dye would break down within one hour.
keep the dye from dissolving further during the exposure.
allow absorbance to be measured without removing the sample from the bath.

why.A: Light intensity is the variable being changed between samples. Holding temperature constant removes it as an explanation for any difference in absorbance, which is what makes the comparison between samples meaningful.
why.B: Treats a controlled variable as if it were the cause under study, and 22 degrees C is close to room temperature rather than elevated.
why.C: Describes an effect on dissolving that the passage never raises; the dye is already in solution.
why.D: Describes a convenience of the apparatus, not a reason to fix the temperature at a particular value.

context: Based on Biologist 2's hypothesis, which frogs would be expected to show the least impact from the decline?

choices.text: Frogs living in ponds farthest from the streams that drain the farmland.
Frogs living in ponds closest to the streams that drain the farmland.
Frogs living in ponds stocked with the invasive fish.
Frogs that have already been exposed to the fungus.

why.A: Biologist 2's hypothesis predicts reproductive success is lowest closest to the farmland drainage streams, so frogs farthest from those streams should be least affected.
why.B: Biologist 2's hypothesis predicts the opposite: reproductive success should be lowest closest to those streams.
why.C: This describes a prediction of Biologist 3's hypothesis, not Biologist 2's.
why.D: This describes a prediction of Biologist 1's hypothesis, not Biologist 2's.

context: Based on Geologist 3's hypothesis, rock outcrops located far apart but within the same regional dust source would most likely have varnish that is—

choices.text: chemically similar only if the rocks underneath are also the same type.
chemically unique to each individual outcrop.
entirely free of the iron and manganese in varnish.
chemically similar to each other, regardless of the type of rock underneath.

why.D: Because Geologist 3 attributes varnish minerals to a shared regional dust source rather than to the underlying rock, outcrops sharing that dust source should have chemically similar varnish regardless of rock type.
why.A: Geologist 3's hypothesis ties varnish composition to the shared dust source, not to the underlying rock type.
why.B: This contradicts Geologist 3's claim that a shared regional dust source should produce similar varnish.
why.C: Geologist 3's hypothesis explains how iron and manganese arrive in the varnish, not their absence.

context: Based on Biologist 3's hypothesis, a pond within Cedar Hollow that has never been stocked with the invasive fish should have:

choices.text: a frog population as sparse as the rest of Cedar Hollow shows.
no frogs at all, regardless of whether fish are present.
a frog population set by fungal presence rather than by the invasive fish.
a relatively dense frog population compared with ponds stocked with the fish.

why.D: Biologist 3 explicitly notes that fish-free ponds within the wetland still support relatively dense frog populations, while stocked ponds show far fewer frogs.
why.A: This contradicts Biologist 3's own observation about fish-free ponds within the wetland.
why.B: Biologist 3's hypothesis ties frog scarcity specifically to the presence of the invasive fish.
why.C: This describes Biologist 1's hypothesis, not Biologist 3's.

context: Suppose two rock outcrops of identical mineral composition are found in two different regions with very different local dust compositions. If Geologist 1's hypothesis alone were correct, the varnish on the two outcrops should be—

choices.text: chemically similar, since the same rock composition would govern both.
chemically different, reflecting each region's own dust.
entirely absent from both of the outcrops.
present on only one of the two outcrops, not both.

why.A: Under Geologist 1's hypothesis alone, varnish composition is governed by the rock's own mineral makeup. Since both outcrops share identical rock composition, their varnish should be chemically similar despite the different regional dust.
why.B: This describes a prediction of Geologist 3's dust-based hypothesis, not Geologist 1's rock-based hypothesis.
why.C: Geologist 1's hypothesis explains how varnish forms on rock containing trace minerals, not its absence.
why.D: Nothing in Geologist 1's hypothesis distinguishes between two outcrops of identical rock composition.

context: All three geologists would most likely agree that desert varnish is composed primarily of—

why.C: The passage's introduction, which precedes and applies to all three geologists' hypotheses, identifies desert varnish as a coating of iron and manganese oxides.
why.A: Calcium carbonate is never named as part of the varnish. It is a common desert mineral, which is what makes it a tempting answer, but the passage does not put it in the coating.
why.B: Silica and quartz are what many of these rocks are made of, not what the coating on them is made of. The question asks about the varnish.
why.D: Organic material appears in the passage only as something bacteria contribute to the process, never as a component of the finished varnish.

context: All three biologists would most likely agree that the decline of the blue-spotted tree frog in Cedar Hollow is:

choices.text: linked to a specific, identifiable cause rather than to random chance.
caused primarily by a fungal skin infection in the frogs.
caused primarily by pesticide runoff from nearby farms.
caused primarily by an invasive predator fish.

why.A: Each biologist proposes a distinct but specific, identifiable mechanism for the decline; none attributes it to unexplained or random variation.
why.B: This is only Biologist 1's specific explanation, not one shared by all three.
why.C: This is only Biologist 2's specific explanation, not one shared by all three.
why.D: This is only Biologist 3's specific explanation, not one shared by all three.

context: Which of the following is a prediction shared by all three geologists' hypotheses?

choices.text: Varnish always matches the composition of the rock beneath it.
Living organisms are required for the varnish to form at all.
The varnish's minerals always come from outside the rock.
Desert varnish accumulates slowly, not quickly.

why.D: All three mechanisms described — slow leaching cycles, gradual bacterial buildup, and continuous dust accumulation — describe a slow, long-term process, consistent with the passage's opening statement that varnish can take centuries to form.
why.A: This prediction follows only from Geologist 1's hypothesis, not from Geologist 2's or Geologist 3's.
why.B: This prediction follows only from Geologist 2's hypothesis, not from Geologist 1's or Geologist 3's.
why.C: This prediction follows from Geologist 2's and Geologist 3's hypotheses but contradicts Geologist 1's.

context: Which of the following, if true, would be equally consistent with the hypotheses of all three biologists?

choices.text: Frogs are absent from every one of the ponds that were stocked with the invasive fish.
The wetland's frog population was significantly larger 20 years ago than it is today.
The fungus has been detected at every site sampled in the wetland.
Reproductive success is lowest in ponds nearest the farmland drainage streams.

why.B: All three biologists are trying to explain the same underlying fact — that the population has fallen substantially over time — so that fact itself is equally consistent with, and does not favor, any one of their three specific hypotheses.
why.A: This specifically supports Biologist 3's hypothesis over the other two.
why.C: This specifically supports Biologist 1's hypothesis over the other two.
why.D: This specifically supports Biologist 2's hypothesis over the other two.

context: Geologist 2's hypothesis depends on bacteria that gain usable energy by chemically oxidizing manganese. This kind of energy-yielding chemical reaction is most similar to—

choices.text: the reaction plants use to convert sunlight into stored chemical energy.
the reaction other bacteria use on iron or sulfur.
the reaction animals use to break down sugar with oxygen for energy.
the physical process by which water freezes into solid ice.

why.B: Bacteria that gain energy by oxidizing inorganic compounds like iron or sulfur use the same general kind of chemical process Geologist 2 describes for manganese — extracting usable energy from oxidizing a chemical compound rather than from light or from digesting sugar.
why.A: That reaction is driven by light rather than by oxidizing a chemical compound.
why.C: That reaction uses a different starting material and does not involve oxidizing a metal.
why.D: Freezing is a physical change of state, not a chemical, energy-yielding reaction.

context: Biologist 2's hypothesis proposes that the pesticide interferes with the frogs' hormone systems. A chemical that disrupts normal hormone signaling in an animal's body is generally known as:

why.D: A chemical that interferes with an animal's hormone signaling is classified as an endocrine disruptor, which is the general term for the kind of substance Biologist 2 describes.
why.A: Pigments used in photosynthesis are unrelated to hormone signaling and occur in plants, not animals.
why.B: A cofactor assists an enzyme's normal function rather than disrupting hormone signaling.
why.C: A structural protein provides physical support in cells and tissues rather than signaling.

context: Finding that frog populations in wetlands downstream of the same farms, but well outside the pesticide's typical travel range, declined just as sharply as Cedar Hollow's population would most directly weaken the hypothesis of:

why.D: Biologist 2's hypothesis predicts less decline farther from the pesticide's reach; a similarly sharp decline well outside that range contradicts that specific prediction.
why.A: This finding does not involve the fungus or its spread in any way.
why.B: This finding does not involve the invasive fish or its presence in any way.
why.C: This finding specifically undercuts the pesticide-exposure mechanism Biologist 2 proposes.

context: The discovery of DNA from manganese-oxidizing bacteria embedded within the varnish layer of several rock samples would most directly support the hypothesis of—

why.A: Geologist 2's hypothesis specifically proposes that manganese-oxidizing bacteria are responsible for the coating, so finding their DNA within the varnish would directly support that view.
why.B: Geologist 1's hypothesis describes a purely chemical process and does not involve living organisms at all.
why.C: Geologist 3's hypothesis describes dust cemented by moisture, not a biological process.
why.D: This finding directly matches the biological mechanism Geologist 2 specifically proposes.

context: Finding that desert varnish forms at measurably different rates on rocks of different mineral composition within the same regional dust environment would most directly support the hypothesis of—

why.C: Only Geologist 1's hypothesis ties the varnish directly to the composition of the rock itself, so a formation rate that varies with rock composition, even under identical regional dust conditions, would support that specific claim.
why.A: Geologist 2's hypothesis ties varnish formation to bacterial colonization rather than to the rock's own mineral composition.
why.B: Geologist 3's hypothesis predicts varnish should depend on the shared regional dust source, not on differences between individual rocks.
why.D: This finding specifically matches Geologist 1's claim that the rock's own composition governs the coating.

context: Chemical analysis showing that a set of rocks' varnish matches the trace-mineral ratios of local windblown dust, but does not match the trace-mineral ratios of the rocks themselves, would most directly weaken the hypothesis of—

why.B: Geologist 1's hypothesis predicts the varnish should match the rock's own mineral makeup. A mismatch with the rock, paired with a match to regional dust, directly contradicts that specific prediction.
why.A: This finding is consistent with an external mineral source, which Geologist 2's hypothesis already proposes.
why.C: This finding directly matches what Geologist 3's hypothesis predicts, so it supports rather than weakens that view.
why.D: The finding specifically contradicts a claim made only by Geologist 1, not by all three.

context: Suppose researchers remove the invasive fish from every pond in Cedar Hollow, and over the following five years frog populations recover to their levels from 20 years ago, even though the fungus remains widespread in the wetland and pesticide use upstream continues unchanged. This outcome would most directly support the hypothesis of:

why.C: Recovery follows fish removal specifically, while the factors central to the other two hypotheses (fungus, pesticide) remain unchanged, so this outcome most directly supports Biologist 3's hypothesis.
why.A: Recovery occurs even though the fungus remains widespread, which does not fit Biologist 1's hypothesis.
why.B: Recovery occurs even though pesticide use continues unchanged, which does not fit Biologist 2's hypothesis.
why.D: Recovery tracks the one variable that did change, fish removal, which is exactly what Biologist 3's hypothesis predicts.

context: Which biologist attributes the frog decline primarily to an infectious disease?

why.D: Biologist 1's hypothesis centers on a fungal skin infection spreading through the frog population.
why.A: Biologist 2's hypothesis centers on pesticide runoff, not infectious disease.
why.B: Biologist 3's hypothesis centers on an invasive predator, not infectious disease.
why.C: Biologist 1 specifically attributes the decline to a fungal skin infection.

context: Which geologist(s) would most likely predict that desert varnish could form on a rock made of pure quartz, a mineral that contains no iron or manganese of its own?

why.C: Geologists 2 and 3 both propose external mineral sources (bacteria absorbing dust-carried metals, or dust itself), so both would predict varnish could form on a rock with no iron or manganese of its own. Geologist 1's hypothesis specifically requires minerals from the rock's own interior.
why.A: Geologist 1's hypothesis specifically requires minerals from within the rock itself, so a mineral-free rock like quartz would prevent varnish from forming under this view.
why.B: Geologist 2 belongs in the answer, but Geologist 1 does not: that hypothesis draws the metals from inside the rock, and pure quartz has none to give.
why.D: This includes all three, but Geologist 1 cannot be among them — that hypothesis needs iron and manganese already in the rock, which is exactly what pure quartz lacks.

context: Geologist 1's hypothesis differs from both Geologist 2's and Geologist 3's primarily in that only Geologist 1 proposes that—

choices.text: desert varnish takes centuries to form.
the varnish darkens in color the longer it is exposed.
living organisms play no role at all in forming any desert coating anywhere.
the varnish minerals come from inside the rock rather than from outside.

why.D: Geologist 1 alone proposes an internal mineral source, migrating outward from the rock; Geologists 2 and 3 both propose external sources — bacteria-processed dust and directly deposited dust, respectively.
why.A: This general timescale is stated in the passage's introduction and is not specific to any one geologist's hypothesis.
why.B: This is also a general observation from the introduction, not a claim distinguishing the three hypotheses.
why.C: Geologist 1's hypothesis makes a claim about this specific coating's chemical origin, not a general claim ruling out biology everywhere.

context: Biologist 1's and Biologist 3's hypotheses differ from Biologist 2's primarily in that only Biologist 2 proposes a mechanism involving:

choices.text: a factor whose effects vary from one pond to another within Cedar Hollow.
a chemical that interferes with reproduction rather than killing frogs.
a cause that arrived in Cedar Hollow within the last 20 years.
a decline that researchers agree has actually occurred.

why.B: Biologist 2 alone proposes a chemical mechanism that reduces reproductive success without necessarily killing frogs outright; Biologist 1 describes a fatal infection and Biologist 3 describes direct predation on eggs and tadpoles.
why.A: Biologist 3's hypothesis also predicts effects that vary from pond to pond, based on fish presence.
why.C: Biologist 3's invasive fish also arrived about 20 years ago, so Biologist 2 is not alone in proposing a recent cause.
why.D: All three biologists agree on the extent of the decline itself.

context: A wetland resembling Cedar Hollow in climate and vegetation, but located far from any farmland and never stocked with the invasive fish, experiences a similar decline shortly after the fungus is detected there for the first time. This finding is most consistent with the view of:

why.A: Because the wetland has no nearby farmland and no invasive fish, the pesticide and predator hypotheses cannot explain its decline; only the fungal hypothesis, tied to the disease's detected arrival, remains consistent with this outcome.
why.B: This wetland has no farmland nearby, ruling out the pesticide-runoff mechanism Biologist 2 proposes.
why.C: This wetland was never stocked with the invasive fish, ruling out the predator mechanism Biologist 3 proposes.
why.D: The scenario specifically rules out the mechanisms proposed by Biologist 2 and Biologist 3.

context: Based on Table 1, if a sample had been exposed at a light intensity of 300 lux, its absorbance after 30 minutes would most likely have been closest to:

why.B: 300 lux falls between the 200 lux reading of 0.71 and the 400 lux reading of 0.54. Absorbance decreases as intensity increases, so the value must lie between 0.54 and 0.71, and 0.63 is the only choice that does.
why.A: Falls below the 400 lux reading, which would require 300 lux to fade the dye faster than 400 lux does.
why.C: Falls above the 200 lux reading, which would require less fading at a higher intensity.
why.D: Is close to the 100 lux reading, ignoring the two rows that actually bracket 300 lux.

context: Using the definition of reaction rate given in the passage and the data in Table 1, what was the reaction rate, in s^-1, for Catalyst X at a concentration of 0.2 mol/L?

why.B: The passage defines rate as 1 divided by time. At 0.2 mol/L, the time is 80 s, so the rate is 1/80 = 0.0125 s^-1.
why.D: Reports the time itself rather than 1 divided by the time.
why.C: Uses the time for 0.4 mol/L (50 s) instead of 0.2 mol/L (80 s).
why.A: Uses the time for 0.1 mol/L (120 s) instead of 0.2 mol/L (80 s).

context: Using the definition given in the passage, what was the relative growth rate, in cm/day, of the seedlings watered every 1 day between day 0 and day 7?

why.B: The passage defines relative growth rate as the change in height divided by days elapsed. From day 0 to day 7, height rose from 0 to 4.9 cm: 4.9 / 7 = 0.7 cm/day.
why.D: Reports the total height change without dividing by the number of days elapsed.
why.C: Doubles the correct rate rather than dividing height change by days elapsed.
why.A: Divides the correct rate in half rather than dividing height change by days elapsed.

context: Using the definition given in the passage and the data in Table 1, what was the frequency, in swings per second, of the pendulum with a string length of 100 cm?

why.C: The passage defines frequency as 1 divided by the period. At a 100 cm string length, the period is 2.0 s, so the frequency is 1/2.0 = 0.5 swings per second.
why.D: Reports the period itself rather than 1 divided by the period.
why.B: Uses a period of 2.5 s rather than the actual 2.0 s recorded for 100 cm.
why.A: Divides the correct frequency in half rather than computing 1 divided by the period.

context: According to Figure 1, which catalyst produced a shorter time to completion at every concentration tested?

choices.text: They were equally fast at every concentration tested.
It varied — each catalyst was faster at some concentrations.

why.B: At every plotted concentration, the Catalyst X curve lies below the Catalyst Y curve, meaning a shorter time to completion.
why.A: Figure 1 shows Catalyst Y's curve above Catalyst X's curve at every concentration, meaning longer times, not shorter.
why.C: The two curves in Figure 1 never touch or cross.
why.D: Catalyst X's curve stays below Catalyst Y's curve across the entire range shown.

context: According to Figure 1, at a concentration of 0.4 mol/L, how much shorter was the time to completion for Catalyst X than for Catalyst Y?

why.A: At 0.4 mol/L, Catalyst Y takes 80 s and Catalyst X takes 50 s; the difference is 80 − 50 = 30 s.
why.B: The time for Catalyst X itself, not the difference between the two catalysts.
why.C: The time for Catalyst Y itself, not the difference between the two catalysts.
why.D: Adds the two times together instead of subtracting.

context: According to Figure 1, on which measured day did the height difference between the two watering groups first exceed 4 cm?

why.D: The height difference is 2.1 cm at day 7 and 5.2 cm at day 14, so day 14 is the first measured day on which it exceeds 4 cm.
why.A: The difference between the two groups at day 7 is only 2.1 cm, under the 4 cm threshold.
why.B: The difference already exceeds 4 cm by day 14, one measurement earlier.
why.C: The difference exceeds 4 cm well before the final measurement.

context: A student claims that, based on Figure 1, doubling the mass of the bob will double the pendulum's period. Do the data in Figure 1 support this claim?

choices.text: Yes, because period is calculated partly from the bob's mass.
Yes, because the heaviest bob (400 g) took visibly longer to complete one swing.
No relevant data on mass were collected in this experiment.
No, because the period stayed at about 2.0 s at every mass tested.

why.D: Correct — Figure 1 shows a period of about 2.0 s at every mass tested, including the 50 g to 100 g and 100 g to 200 g doublings, so the claim is not supported.
why.A: The passage never defines period in terms of mass, and Figure 1's data show no such relationship.
why.B: Figure 1 shows the 400 g bob's period matching every other mass tested, not exceeding it.
why.C: Figure 1 specifically reports period at five different bob masses.

context: Based on the data in Table 1, the time to completion for Catalyst X at a concentration of 0.3 mol/L would most likely be closest to—

why.B: A concentration of 0.3 mol/L falls exactly halfway between the 0.2 mol/L row (80 s) and the 0.4 mol/L row (50 s), so the estimated time is halfway between them: 80 − (80 − 50)/2 = 65 s.
why.A: The reading for 0.4 mol/L, one row past the value being asked about.
why.C: The reading for 0.2 mol/L, one row before the value being asked about.
why.D: Adds, rather than subtracts, half the difference between the two bracketing rows.

context: Based on Figure 1, the height of the seedlings watered every 4 days on day 17.5 would most likely be closest to—

why.C: Day 17.5 falls exactly halfway between day 14 (6.4 cm) and day 21 (10.5 cm), so the estimated height is halfway between them: 6.4 + (10.5-6.4)/2 = 8.45 cm.
why.A: The reading for day 14, one measurement before the day being asked about.
why.D: The reading for day 21, one measurement after the day being asked about.
why.B: Averages the two nearest readings incorrectly rather than interpolating proportionally.

context: Based on the data in Table 1, the period of the pendulum for a string length of 75 cm would most likely be closest to:

why.C: A string length of 75 cm falls exactly halfway between the 50 cm row (1.4 s) and the 100 cm row (2.0 s), so the estimated period is halfway between them: 1.4 + (2.0-1.4)/2 = 1.7 s.
why.A: The reading for a 50 cm string length, one row before the value being asked about.
why.D: The reading for a 100 cm string length, one row after the value being asked about.
why.B: A plausible-looking value that does not fall halfway between the two bracketing rows.

context: According to Table 1, what was the time to completion for Catalyst X at a concentration of 0.4 mol/L?

why.C: Table 1 lists 50 s in the row for a concentration of 0.4 mol/L.
