why.C: This divides by 10, which is not the seconds-to-minutes relationship.
why.D: 2 minutes is 120 s, which is the second-to-last reading rather than the final one.

context: What was the average rate of CO₂ production during the first 30 seconds of Study 2?

why.A: Correct — 22 mL collected in 30 s gives 22 ÷ 30 ≈ 0.73 mL/s.
why.B: 22 mL is the total volume for the interval, not a rate; it still has to be divided by the time.
why.C: 0.37 mL/s is the average across the whole 150 s, which is slower because production tails off.
why.D: This divides 30 by 22, inverting the rate into seconds per milliliter.

context: During which interval was CO₂ produced most rapidly?

why.A: Correct — 22 mL appeared in this interval, more than in any other 30-second span.
why.B: This interval added 16 mL, less than the first.
why.C: This interval added only 6 mL.
why.D: This interval added just 2 mL, the slowest of all.

context: What was the average rate of CO₂ production across the entire 150 seconds?

why.A: Correct — 56 mL total divided by 150 s gives about 0.37 mL/s.
why.B: 0.73 mL/s is the rate during the first 30 s only, when production was fastest.
why.C: This would require 150 mL of gas, nearly three times what was collected.
why.D: 0.07 mL/s is roughly the rate in the final interval, not the average over the whole run.

context: How does the rate of CO₂ production change over the course of Study 2?

choices.text: It stays roughly constant until the reaction stops.

why.A: Correct — successive 30-second intervals add 22, 16, 10, 6, and 2 mL, a falling amount each time.
why.B: The amounts added fall rather than rise; only the running total increases.
why.C: A constant rate would add equal volumes each interval, but the first adds eleven times what the last does.
why.D: There is no early rise; the fastest interval is the very first one.

context: In the still-air trial with the lamp on, what was the average rate of water loss per hour?

why.A: Correct — 1.40 g lost over 3 hours gives 1.40 ÷ 3 ≈ 0.47 g/h.
why.B: This multiplies by 3 instead of dividing, giving the loss for nine hours.
why.C: 1.40 g is the total for the whole trial, not the amount per hour.
why.D: This divides by 6, as though the trial had run for six hours.

context: By approximately what factor did moving air increase the rate of water loss compared with still air, with the lamp on in both trials?

why.A: Correct — 2.35 g against 1.40 g over the same 3 hours gives a ratio of about 1.7.
why.B: This is the reciprocal, 1.40 ÷ 2.35, which would mean the fan slowed the loss.
why.C: This roughly doubles the correct ratio; 3.4 times 1.40 would be well above the measured 2.35 g.
why.D: A factor of 1.0 would mean the fan made no difference, but the loss rose by nearly a gram.

context: Across the full range tested in Study 1, what was the average change in dissolution time for each 10 °C rise in water temperature?

why.A: Correct — the time fell from 180 s to 40 s, a change of 140 s spread over four 10-degree steps, so 140 ÷ 4 = 35 s per step.
why.B: 140 s is the total change across the whole range, not the change per step.
why.C: This divides 140 by 5, the number of temperatures tested, rather than by the 4 intervals between them.
why.D: This divides by 40, mixing up the degrees with the number of steps.

context: What was the approximate rate of CO₂ production between 120 s and 150 s?

why.A: Correct — the total rose from 54 mL to 56 mL, so 2 mL over 30 s is about 0.07 mL/s.
why.B: 0.2 mL/s is the rate in the preceding interval, when 6 mL was produced.
why.C: 2 mL is the volume added during the interval, not the rate per second.
why.D: This divides the running total of 56 mL by 30 s, ignoring the gas already collected.

context: What total volume of CO₂ had been collected once the readings stopped changing?

why.A: Correct — Table 2 reports a running total, and its final value is 56 mL.
why.B: 54 mL is the reading at 120 s, before the last 2 mL appeared.
why.C: This adds every reading together, but the column is already cumulative.
why.D: 2 mL is the amount added in the final interval, not the total.

context: How much CO₂ was produced between 30 s and 90 s?

why.A: Correct — the total rose from 22 mL to 48 mL, a difference of 26 mL.
why.B: This adds the two readings rather than subtracting them.
why.C: 48 mL is the running total at 90 s, which includes gas produced before 30 s.
why.D: 10 mL is the amount added between 60 s and 90 s alone.

context: How many seconds faster did a powdered tablet dissolve than a whole one?

why.A: Correct — 120 s for the whole tablet minus 45 s for the powder gives 75 s.
why.B: 45 s is the powder's own dissolution time, not the difference.
why.C: 95 s is the time for the halved tablet.
why.D: 25 s is the difference between the whole tablet and the halved one.

context: What is the difference in dissolution time between water at 10 °C and water at 30 °C?

why.A: Correct — 180 s at 10 °C minus 80 s at 30 °C equals 100 s.
why.B: 60 s is the difference between 10 °C and 20 °C.
why.C: 140 s is the difference between the extremes, 10 °C and 50 °C.
why.D: 40 s is the difference between 20 °C and 30 °C.

context: In Study 3, how much greater was the mass change in 3.5% NaCl than in distilled water?

why.A: Correct — 0.41 g minus 0.18 g equals 0.23 g.
why.B: This adds the two values instead of subtracting them.
why.C: This subtracts the 0.5% result, 0.26 g, from 0.41 g rather than the 0.0% result.
why.D: 0.41 g is the mass change at 3.5% on its own, not the difference.

context: For the 8-leaf cutting in still air, what was the average water loss per leaf over the 3 hours?

why.A: Correct — 1.40 g divided among 8 leaves gives 0.175 g per leaf.
why.B: 0.08 g is the loss measured from the leafless cutting, which came through the stem.
why.C: This multiplies 1.40 by 8 rather than dividing.
why.D: This divides by 4 instead of 8.

context: Coating the lower leaf surfaces reduced water loss by approximately what percentage of the untreated value?

why.A: Correct — the loss fell from 1.40 g to 0.45 g, a drop of 0.95 g, and 0.95 ÷ 1.40 is about 68%.
why.B: 32% is the fraction of the original loss that remained, not the reduction.
why.C: This treats the remaining 0.45 g as a percentage without dividing by the original.
why.D: 86% would leave only about 0.20 g, which is the result for coating both surfaces.

context: What percentage of the total CO₂ had been collected by 90 seconds?

why.A: Correct — 48 mL of the eventual 56 mL is about 86%.
why.B: 48 is the volume in milliliters, not a percentage.
why.C: About 68% corresponds to the 38 mL reading at 60 s.
why.D: 96% would be about 54 mL, the reading at 120 s.

context: A student hypothesized that sandstone with more pore space cracks after fewer freezing cycles. Do the results of Experiment 1 support this hypothesis?

choices.text: Yes; as porosity rises from 4% to 18%, the cycles to first crack fall from 210 to 30.
Yes; as porosity rises from 4% to 18%, the cycles to first crack rise from 30 to 210.
No; porosity and cycles to first crack both increase together.

why.A: Correct — Table 1 shows fewer cycles needed at higher porosity, which is exactly what the hypothesis predicts.
why.B: Reads the table backwards. The 210-cycle core is the 4% one, the least porous.
why.C: The two move in opposite directions, not together.
why.D: Porosity is the variable Experiment 1 varies; it is held constant in Experiments 2 and 3.

context: Experiment 3 was designed to test which hypothesis?

choices.text: That cracking requires water inside the pore spaces, not merely repeated cooling.
That cracking depends on the porosity of the sandstone.
That cracking occurs faster when the maximum temperature of the cycle is set higher.
That sandstone cracks more readily than other rock types.

why.A: Correct — Experiment 3 changes only one thing from Experiment 2: the cores are dried. That isolates the role of pore water.
why.B: Porosity was held at 12% throughout Experiment 3, so it cannot be what the experiment tests.
why.C: The maximum stayed at +5 °C in every experiment described.
why.D: Only sandstone was tested; no comparison with another rock type appears anywhere in the studies.

context: The results of Experiment 3 are most consistent with which statement?

choices.text: Freezing temperatures alone are not sufficient to crack sandstone.
Freezing temperatures alone are sufficient to crack sandstone.
Dried sandstone cracks more slowly, but still cracks within 300 cycles.
Cracking depends only on how far below 0 °C the rock is taken.

why.A: Correct — dried cores taken to −20 °C 300 times showed no cracks at all, so the cold by itself did not do the damage.
why.B: If cold alone were sufficient, the dried cores would have cracked. None did.
why.C: Table 3 reports zero cracks, not slower cracking.
why.D: This is the claim Experiment 3 rules out: the dried cores reached the same temperatures and survived.

context: Experiment 2 was most likely designed to test the hypothesis that:

choices.text: how cold the rock gets during a cycle affects how quickly it cracks.
how porous the rock is affects how quickly it cracks.
how long a core is soaked before cycling affects how quickly it cracks.
dried cores crack at the same rate as soaked cores.

why.A: Correct — Experiment 2 varies the minimum temperature and holds porosity fixed at 12%, so the minimum temperature is what it is testing.
why.B: That is Experiment 1. Experiment 2 uses a single porosity.
why.C: The 48-hour soak was the same for every soaked core; it was never varied.
why.D: That comparison belongs to Experiment 3.

context: A geologist hypothesizes that once the minimum temperature is below −10 °C, cooling the rock further has no additional effect on how quickly it cracks. Do the results of Experiment 2 support this?

choices.text: No; cycles to first crack fall from 65 to 40 as the minimum drops from −10 °C to −20 °C.
Yes; cycles to first crack are the same at −10 °C and −20 °C.
Yes; no cores cracked at temperatures below −10 °C.
No; cycles to first crack rise from 40 to 65 as the minimum drops from −10 °C to −20 °C.

why.A: Correct — a further drop still shortened the time to cracking, so the additional cooling did have an effect.
why.B: Table 2 gives 65 at −10 °C and 40 at −20 °C, which are not the same.
why.C: The −20 °C cores cracked sooner than any others in Experiment 2.
why.D: Reverses the direction. Colder minimums produced cracking in fewer cycles, not more.

context: Which result would most weaken the hypothesis that expanding pore ice is what breaks the rock?

choices.text: Soaked cores cycled between +5 °C and +2 °C crack after about 65 cycles.
Soaked cores of 25% porosity crack after only about 20 freeze-thaw cycles.
Dried cores cycled 600 times at −20 °C still show no cracks.
Soaked cores cycled to −30 °C crack after about 32 cycles.

why.A: Correct — water in the pores never freezes on that cycle, so cracking without any ice would undercut the proposed mechanism.
why.B: This extends the porosity trend of Experiment 1 and fits the mechanism rather than challenging it.
why.C: This reinforces the mechanism: without pore water there is no ice, and no cracking.
why.D: This extends the temperature trend of Experiment 2 and is consistent with the mechanism.

context: In Experiment 1, which variable was deliberately varied between cores?

choices.text: The minimum temperature of the freezing cycle
The length of time each core was soaked
The number of cycles each core received

why.A: Correct — four sandstones of differing porosity were cut into cores and otherwise treated identically.
why.B: The cycle ran between +5 °C and −10 °C for every core in Experiment 1. Varying the minimum is Experiment 2.
why.C: Every core was soaked for 48 hours.
why.D: Cycles were counted, not set in advance; cores were inspected after every cycle until one cracked.

context: Which variable was varied in Experiment 1 but held constant in Experiment 2?

why.A: Correct — Experiment 1 used four porosities; Experiment 2 used only 12% cores.
why.B: This runs the other way: it was fixed in Experiment 1 and varied in Experiment 2.
why.C: The maximum was +5 °C in both experiments, so it was not varied in either.
why.D: Soaking time was 48 hours in both.

context: Experiment 3 differed from Experiment 2 in which single respect?

choices.text: The cores had a different porosity.
The cycle ran between different maximum and minimum temperatures.
The cores were inspected only once rather than after every cycle.

why.A: Correct — the porosity, the temperatures and the cycling were carried over unchanged; only the water was removed, and the cores were kept dry instead of soaked.
why.B: Both experiments used 12% porosity cores.
why.C: Experiment 3 repeated the same set of minimum temperatures used in Experiment 2.
why.D: Nothing in the description changes the inspection schedule; in any case no cracks appeared to find.

context: A 12% porosity core cycled to a minimum of −10 °C appears in both Experiment 1 and Experiment 2. What do the two results show?

choices.text: Experiment 1 reports 65 cycles and Experiment 2 reports 130, a discrepancy.
Experiment 1 reports 210 cycles and Experiment 2 reports 65.
Only Experiment 2 tested that combination, so no comparison is possible.

why.A: Correct — the 12% row of Table 1 and the −10 °C row of Table 2 describe the same conditions and give the same figure.
why.B: 130 is the Experiment 2 value for a −5 °C minimum, not −10 °C.
why.C: 210 is the Experiment 1 value for 4% porosity, not 12%.
why.D: Experiment 1 ran every core to a −10 °C minimum, and one of those cores was 12% porosity.

context: Suppose a core of 15% porosity had been included in Experiment 1. Based on Table 1, it would most likely have cracked after how many cycles?

why.A: Fewer than 30 cycles would put a 15% core past the 18% core, but it is less porous than that one.
why.B: Correct — 15% falls between the 12% core (65 cycles) and the 18% core (30 cycles), so its value falls between theirs.
why.C: This range belongs to cores less porous than 12%.
why.D: More than 210 cycles is beyond even the least porous core tested.

context: The mechanism these experiments investigate depends on an unusual property of water. Which statement describes it?

choices.text: Water expands when it freezes, whereas most substances contract on solidifying.
Water contracts when it freezes, just as most other substances do.
Water changes directly from liquid to gas at 0 °C.
Water conducts heat better as a solid than nearly any other common material.

why.A: Correct — ice occupies more volume than the water it came from, which is why freezing inside a sealed pore pushes outward on the rock.
why.B: If water contracted on freezing, it would pull away from the pore walls rather than press against them, and the proposed mechanism would not work.
why.C: 0 °C is water's freezing point. The liquid-to-gas change is boiling, at 100 °C at sea level.
why.D: Thermal conductivity is not what breaks the rock here; the expansion of the ice is.

context: Pure water at ordinary pressure freezes at 0 °C. Which minimum temperature used in Experiment 2 would leave pore water closest to the point of not freezing at all?

why.A: Correct — it is the minimum nearest 0 °C, and the cores cycled to it took the most cycles to crack, 240.
why.B: Colder than −2 °C, and further from the freezing point.
why.C: This is the standard minimum used in Experiment 1, not the one nearest freezing.
why.D: This is the coldest minimum tested, the furthest from 0 °C.

context: Dissolved salt lowers the temperature at which water freezes. If the cores in Experiment 2 had been soaked in salt water instead of pure water, the cycles to first crack at a minimum of −2 °C would most likely have:

choices.text: increased, because the pore water might not freeze at −2 °C at all.
decreased, because salt water expands more than pure water on freezing.
stayed at 240, because salt does not enter the pore spaces.
decreased, because salt water freezes at a higher temperature.

why.A: Correct — with the freezing point pushed below −2 °C, some or all cycles would produce no ice, and cracking would take longer or not occur.
why.B: Nothing here suggests salt water expands more; the relevant effect is on when it freezes.
why.C: The cores are soaked, so whatever is dissolved in the water enters the pores with it.
why.D: Salt lowers the freezing point rather than raising it.

context: The second column of Table 1 reports its values in which units?

choices.text: Cycles, a count of completed freeze-and-thaw repetitions
Degrees Celsius, a unit of temperature
Percent, a proportion of the rock's original volume

why.A: Correct — the column heading reads "Cycles to first crack," and a cycle is one full pass between the two temperatures.
why.B: No time in seconds is reported anywhere in these studies.
why.C: Degrees Celsius label the temperatures in Table 2 and Table 3, not this column.
why.D: Percent is the unit of the porosity column, the first one.

context: The chamber completes one cycle per hour. Approximately how long did a 12% porosity core take to crack in Experiment 1?

why.A: Treats each cycle as a minute rather than an hour.
why.B: Correct — 65 cycles at one per hour is 65 hours, which is a little under 3 days.
why.C: Three weeks would be over 500 hours, far more than 65 cycles.
why.D: Treats each cycle as a day rather than an hour.

context: A summary of Experiment 2 reports one of the minimum temperatures as 263 K. Given that a temperature in kelvins is the Celsius value plus 273, which row of Table 2 does this describe?

why.A: −2 °C corresponds to about 271 K.
why.B: −5 °C corresponds to about 268 K.
why.D: −20 °C corresponds to about 253 K.

context: According to Table 3, which soil took in water fastest during the final interval of the test?

why.A: Correct — sand's rate of 180 mm/hr is the largest of the three.
why.B: Loam's 66 mm/hr is well below sand's.
why.C: Clay's 18 mm/hr is the smallest of the three.
why.D: The two differ by more than a factor of two.

context: During the first 5 minutes of the test, at what average rate did water soak into the sand?

why.A: Reports the elapsed time rather than the rate.
why.B: Correct — 45 mm of water soaked in over 5 minutes, and 45 ÷ 5 = 9 mm/min.
why.C: This is the total depth over the interval, not the rate per minute.
why.D: Multiplies depth by time instead of dividing.

context: For loam, how does the average rate of infiltration over the 20–40 minute interval compare with the rate over the first 5 minutes?

choices.text: It is lower: about 1.1 mm/min compared with 4 mm/min.
It is higher: about 4 mm/min compared with 1.1 mm/min.
It is unchanged at about 2 mm/min throughout.
It cannot be compared, because Table 1 reports totals rather than rates.

why.A: Correct — loam gained 20 mm in the first 5 minutes (4 mm/min) and 22 mm over the last 20 minutes (1.1 mm/min).
why.B: Reverses the two intervals. Infiltration slows as the test goes on.
why.C: The rate falls by roughly a factor of four across the test.
why.D: Rates follow from totals: the change in cumulative depth divided by the time it took.

context: Do the clay figures in Table 1 for the 20–40 minute interval agree with the rate reported for clay in Table 3?

choices.text: Yes; 6 mm over 20 minutes is 0.3 mm/min, which is 18 mm/hr.
No; 6 mm over 20 minutes is 0.3 mm/hr, not 18 mm/hr.
No; 21 mm over 40 minutes is 31.5 mm/hr, not 18 mm/hr.
Yes; 15 mm over 20 minutes is 45 mm/hr, which rounds to 18 mm/hr.

why.A: Correct — clay rose from 15 mm to 21 mm, a gain of 6 mm in 20 minutes, and 0.3 mm/min × 60 = 18 mm/hr.
why.B: Confuses per-minute with per-hour. Converting between them is the step that produces 18.
why.C: This is the average over the whole test, not the final interval Table 3 reports.
why.D: 15 mm is the cumulative total at 20 minutes, not the gain during the final interval.

context: By approximately what factor does sand's final infiltration rate exceed clay's?

why.A: This is closer to the ratio between loam and clay, 66 to 18.
why.B: Correct — 180 mm/hr ÷ 18 mm/hr = 10.
why.C: This is the difference between the two rates, not the factor by which one exceeds the other.
why.D: Multiplies the two rates instead of dividing.

context: For how many of the three soils is the final-interval rate in Table 3 lower than that soil's average rate across the whole 40-minute test?

why.A: Every soil's cumulative curve flattens as the test goes on, which is exactly what a falling rate looks like.
why.B: Sand, loam, and clay all show the same pattern, not just one of them.
why.C: The third soil behaves the same way as the other two.
why.D: Correct — the whole-test averages are about 285, 111, and 32 mm/hr, each above the 180, 66, and 18 mm/hr of the final interval.

context: After 40 minutes, how much more water had soaked into the sand than into the clay?

why.A: This is the clay total alone.
why.B: Subtracts the wrong pair: sand at 20 minutes minus clay at 20 minutes gives 115.
why.C: Correct — 190 mm − 21 mm = 169 mm.
why.D: Adds the two totals instead of subtracting.

context: What percentage of the sand's 40-minute total had already soaked in by the 10-minute mark?

why.A: 25% would correspond to about 48 mm, which is closer to the 5-minute reading.
why.B: Correct — 80 mm of the eventual 190 mm is 80 ÷ 190 ≈ 42%.
why.C: 68% would be about 130 mm, the reading at 20 minutes rather than 10.
why.D: Reads the 80 mm value as a percentage.

context: How much water soaked into the loam between the 10-minute and 20-minute readings?

why.A: Correct — the cumulative figures are 34 mm and 52 mm, a gain of 18 mm.
why.B: This is the cumulative total at 10 minutes, not the gain over the interval.
why.C: This is the cumulative total at 20 minutes.
why.D: Adds the two cumulative readings instead of subtracting.

context: If clay continued to take in water at the rate given for it in Table 3, what would its cumulative infiltration be at 60 minutes?

why.A: Adds only 3 mm, the gain over 10 further minutes rather than 20.
why.B: Correct — 18 mm/hr for the extra 20 minutes adds 6 mm to the 21 mm already recorded.
why.C: Adds a full hour's worth of infiltration, 18 mm, rather than 20 minutes' worth.
why.D: Doubles the 40-minute total.

context: At the 40-minute reading, the gap between loam and clay is approximately how many times the gap between them at the 5-minute reading?

why.A: Two times would put the 40-minute gap near 28 mm; it is 53 mm.
why.B: Correct — the gaps are 74 − 21 = 53 mm and 20 − 6 = 14 mm, and 53 ÷ 14 ≈ 3.8.
why.C: Eight times would require a 40-minute gap of over 100 mm.
why.D: Reuses the 5-minute gap of 14 mm as though it were the factor.

context: At the 20-minute reading, the loam's cumulative infiltration is closest to what fraction of the sand's?

why.A: One-eighth of 130 mm is about 16 mm, which is close to the clay reading, not the loam one.
why.B: One-quarter of 130 mm is about 33 mm, below the loam's 52 mm.
why.C: Correct — 52 mm out of 130 mm is exactly 0.4.
why.D: Three-quarters would be about 98 mm, far above the loam reading.

context: Bulk density in Table 2 is reported in g/cm³. This unit expresses:

choices.text: a percentage of the sample's total weight.

why.A: Correct — grams measure mass and cubic centimeters measure volume, so the ratio is mass per volume.
why.B: That would be cm³/g, the reciprocal of what is given.
why.C: Area would be a squared length, such as cm², not a cubed one.
why.D: Percentages are the unit of the organic matter and clay content columns.

context: Sand's rate in Table 3 is 180 mm/hr. Expressed in millimeters per minute, this rate is:

why.A: Divides by 100 rather than by 60.
why.B: Correct — an hour holds 60 minutes, so 180 ÷ 60 = 3 mm/min.
why.C: Divides by 10 rather than by 60.
why.D: Multiplies by 60. Converting to a shorter time interval makes the number smaller, not larger.

context: According to Table 2, which soil has the greatest clay content?

why.A: 4% is the smallest of the three values.
why.B: 19% is larger than sand's but well below clay's.
why.C: Correct — 52% is the largest value in the clay content column.
why.D: The two differ by 33 percentage points.

context: Across the three soils, how does the final-interval infiltration rate change as clay content increases?

why.A: Correct — clay content of 4%, 19%, and 52% pairs with rates of 180, 66, and 18 mm/hr.
why.B: The rates fall as clay content rises, not the reverse.
why.C: There is no turning point; each step down in rate follows a step up in clay content.
why.D: The pattern holds for all three soils without exception.

context: Which soil has both the lowest bulk density and the highest organic matter content?

why.A: Sand has the highest bulk density, 1.55 g/cm³, and the lowest organic matter, 0.8%.
why.B: Correct — loam's 1.32 g/cm³ is the lowest bulk density and its 3.6% is the highest organic matter.
why.C: Clay is in the middle on both measures.
why.D: One soil does hold both extremes, which is what makes the pairing worth noticing.

context: According to Scientist 1, the trout disappeared primarily because:

choices.text: the band of water cold enough for trout grew thinner each summer until it closed.
phosphorus washed from farmland fed algae whose decay used up the deep layer's oxygen.
the deep layer of the lake warmed past the temperature that trout are able to tolerate.
trout were caught faster than they could reproduce.

why.A: Correct — Scientist 1 describes a warming surface and a sinking boundary squeezing the habitable band until it closed in the hottest years.
why.B: This is Scientist 2's account, not Scientist 1's.
why.C: Scientist 1 points to the surface layer warming and expanding downward; Table 1 shows the deep layer holding near 6 °C.
why.D: Neither scientist raises fishing pressure as a cause.

context: Scientist 2 attributes the loss of the trout to:

choices.text: a rise of 2.6 °C in the lake's August surface temperature.
oxygen loss in the deep layer, driven by nutrients running off expanded farmland.
the disappearance of the cold deep layer during the hottest summers since records began.
a decline in the algae the trout depend on for food.

why.A: Scientist 2 names this figure only to argue it is too small to explain the loss on its own.
why.B: Correct — doubled farm acreage raised phosphorus, phosphorus fed algae, and decaying algae consumed the deep layer's oxygen.
why.C: Scientist 2 argues the opposite: the cold water never disappeared, it became unbreathable.
why.D: In Scientist 2's account algae increased, and their increase is the problem rather than a food supply.

context: Which statement would both scientists accept?

choices.text: Oxygen in the lake's deep layer declined over the period studied.
The decline in oxygen was caused by a longer stratified season.
Phosphorus entering the lake rose after 1990.
The deep layer became too warm for trout.

why.A: Correct — Scientist 2 builds the argument on it and Scientist 1 concedes it outright, disagreeing only about its cause.
why.B: This is Scientist 1's explanation for the oxygen decline, and it is precisely what Scientist 2 rejects as the primary story.
why.C: Scientist 2 asserts this; Scientist 1 never addresses farm acreage at all.
why.D: Neither scientist claims this, and Table 1 shows the deep layer steady near 6 °C.

context: How does Scientist 1 account for the fall in deep-layer oxygen?

choices.text: As a measurement artifact that does not reflect a real change.
As the direct cause of the decline, agreeing with Scientist 2 on that particular point.
As the result of the trout themselves consuming more oxygen as the water warmed up further.

why.A: Scientist 1 accepts the fall as real and offers a cause for it.
why.B: Correct — a warmer, longer-stratified summer cuts the deep layer off from the air for longer, which is how Scientist 1 folds the oxygen data into a warming explanation.
why.C: Scientist 1 treats the oxygen fall as a consequence of warming rather than as the primary cause.
why.D: No such claim appears; a declining fish population would in any case consume less oxygen, not more.

context: Which finding, if confirmed, would most weaken Scientist 2's explanation?

choices.text: Phosphorus inputs held steady from 1990 to 2020.
Algae in Lake Idris grew more abundant each decade after 1990.
Lab trout stop feeding below 4 mg/L of oxygen at any temperature.
August surface temperature rose faster after 2010 than before it.

why.A: Correct — the phosphorus increase is the first link in Scientist 2's chain. Remove it and the algae, the decay, and the oxygen loss lose their proposed source.
why.B: More algae is what Scientist 2 predicts, so this supports the account.
why.C: This supports Scientist 2 by confirming that the measured oxygen levels are low enough to matter.
why.D: This bears on Scientist 1's timeline and leaves the nutrient argument untouched.

context: A nearby lake warmed by the same amount over the same period but has no farmland in its watershed, and its trout population is unchanged. This finding would:

choices.text: support Scientist 1, because it shows warming of this kind is widespread across the region.
weaken both accounts, because neither predicts a lake that keeps its trout.
have no bearing, because the two lakes are not the same size.

why.A: Correct — the comparison lake isolates warming from runoff, and warming alone was not enough to cost it its trout, which is Scientist 2’s central claim.
why.B: Whether warming is widespread is not in dispute. What the comparison tests is whether warming alone suffices, and here it did not.
why.C: Scientist 2 predicts exactly this outcome for a lake without added nutrients.
why.D: Size is never raised by either scientist, and the comparison controls the one variable that matters to the dispute.

context: Scientist 2 answers the warming argument chiefly by pointing out that:

choices.text: surface temperature in Lake Idris was never measured accurately at all before 2000.
the deep layer remained near 6 °C in August, so cold water was still available.
lake trout can tolerate water as warm as 22 °C for short periods.
the catch fell even in the years when the summer was unusually cool.

why.A: Scientist 2 disputes the significance of the temperature rise, not the measurements themselves.
why.B: Correct — the argument is that a 2.6 °C surface rise cannot remove a deep layer that is still 6 °C, so the cold habitat persisted and something else made it unusable.
why.C: Neither scientist makes any claim about trout tolerating 22 °C water.
why.D: It is Scientist 1 who ties the steepest drops to the hottest summers; Scientist 2 does not contest that pairing.

context: Which prediction follows from both scientists' accounts?

choices.text: A species tolerating both warm water and low oxygen would not have declined in Lake Idris.
A fish species that requires cold water but tolerates low oxygen would have declined.
A fish species that requires high oxygen but tolerates warm water would also have declined.
Every fish species in Lake Idris would have declined at the same rate as the trout.

why.A: Correct — it escapes both proposed causes, so neither account predicts trouble for it.
why.B: Scientist 1 would predict a decline, but Scientist 2 would not, since such a fish could live in the deoxygenated cold layer.
why.C: Scientist 2 would predict a decline, but Scientist 1 would not, since such a fish could live in the warm surface layer.
why.D: Both accounts turn on the specific requirements of the trout, so species with different tolerances would fare differently.

context: Which column of Table 1 most directly tests Scientist 2's hypothesis?

why.A: Surface temperature is the measurement Scientist 1's hypothesis turns on.
why.B: Scientist 2 cites this column only to show the cold water persisted, not as the proposed cause.
why.C: Correct — Scientist 2's claim is that oxygen in the deep layer fell below what trout require, and this column is the measurement of exactly that.
why.D: The catch is the outcome both scientists are trying to explain, so it cannot distinguish between them.

context: Scientist 1's account predicts what about the boundary between the warm and cold layers over the period studied?

choices.text: It rose steadily toward the surface.
It stayed at a constant depth.

why.A: Correct — a deepening boundary is what thins the cold band from above, which is the mechanism Scientist 1 describes.
why.B: A rising boundary would give the trout more cold water, not less.
why.C: A constant boundary would leave the habitable band the same width each summer, and the account requires it to narrow.
why.D: Scientist 1 says the cold band closed in the hottest years, not that the lake stopped separating into layers at all.

context: In which year did the deep-layer oxygen measurement first fall below the threshold Scientist 2 identifies as the trout's requirement?

why.A: The 2000 reading is 6.7 mg/L, well above the stated requirement.
why.B: The 2005 reading is 5.2 mg/L, still above it.
why.C: Correct — Scientist 2 gives 4 mg/L as the requirement, and 2010 is the first year the measurement, 3.8 mg/L, falls below it.
why.D: The 2015 reading of 2.6 mg/L is below the threshold, but it is not the first year that happened.

context: Suppose the deep-layer temperature column in Table 1 had instead risen from 5.8 °C in 1995 to 12 °C in 2020. What effect would this have on the two accounts?

choices.text: It would strengthen Scientist 1 and undercut a key claim of Scientist 2.
It would strengthen Scientist 2 and undercut a key claim of Scientist 1.
It would strengthen both accounts equally.
It would have no effect on either account.

why.A: Correct — Scientist 2 insists the cold water persisted and only became unbreathable; a deep layer at 12 °C would no longer be cold enough for trout, which is Scientist 1's picture of a closing habitable band.
why.B: Scientist 2's argument depends on the deep layer staying cold, so warming it to 12 °C works against that account.
why.C: The two accounts make opposite predictions about this column, so one measurement cannot favor both.
why.D: Whether cold water remained available is the exact point on which the two accounts differ.

context: Dissolved oxygen is reported in milligrams per liter. A reading of 1.9 mg/L means that:

choices.text: each liter of lake water contains 1.9 milligrams of dissolved oxygen.
1.9% of the water in the lake is oxygen by volume.
each milligram of the lake water holds 1.9 liters of dissolved oxygen.
the lake as a whole contains 1.9 milligrams of oxygen.

why.A: Correct — the unit is a mass of oxygen per volume of water, so 1.9 mg of oxygen accompanies every liter.
why.B: A percentage by volume would be a unitless proportion, not a mass per volume.
why.C: Inverts the unit. The milligrams measure oxygen and the liters measure water.
why.D: The unit describes a concentration, which does not depend on how large the lake is.

context: Bacteria that break down dead organic matter consume oxygen as they do so. This fact is most directly relevant to:

choices.text: Scientist 2's claim that decaying algae drew down the deep layer's oxygen.
Scientist 1's claim that the habitable cold band grew narrower each summer.
Scientist 1's claim that the decline tracked air temperature year for year.
Scientist 2's claim that the deep layer stayed near 6 °C.

why.A: Correct — decay consuming oxygen is the step that connects the algae to the oxygen readings in Scientist 2's chain.
why.B: The width of the cold band depends on temperature, not on decomposition.
why.C: The year-by-year tracking is an argument from timing, and bacteria do not bear on it.
why.D: The deep layer's temperature is a physical measurement, unaffected by what bacteria consume.

context: Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen than cold water does. A student argues that this fact alone explains the fall in deep-layer oxygen in Table 1. Which observation most weakens the student’s argument?

choices.text: The deep layer stayed near 6 °C while its oxygen fell from 8.1 to 1.9 mg/L.
Surface temperature rose by 2.6 °C over the same years that deep-layer oxygen fell.
The trout catch fell from 1,240 fish in 1995 to none at all by 2020.
Deep-layer oxygen had dropped below the 4 mg/L trout need by 2010.

why.A: Correct — the deep water’s own temperature barely moved (5.8 to 6.1 °C), so its capacity to hold oxygen barely changed; something else removed the oxygen.
why.B: Surface warming happens in a different layer and, if anything, looks like support for a temperature explanation.
why.C: The catch shows the consequence of low oxygen, not what caused the oxygen to fall.
why.D: This dates when oxygen became too low for trout but says nothing about why it fell.

context: Phosphorus is a common ingredient in agricultural fertilizer. Knowing this makes which part of the discussion easier to follow?

choices.text: Why doubling farm acreage would raise the phosphorus entering the lake.
Why the deep layer of the lake stays colder all summer than the surface.
Why lake trout require dissolved oxygen above 4 mg/L in order to keep feeding.
Why the August surface temperature of the lake rose by 2.6 °C.

why.A: Correct — it supplies the missing link between more farmland and more phosphorus, which Scientist 2 states but does not explain.
why.B: Layering in a lake follows from the density of water at different temperatures, not from fertilizer.
why.C: The oxygen requirement is a property of the fish, unrelated to what enters the watershed.
why.D: The temperature rise is attributed to climate, and no part of either account routes it through fertilizer.

context: In summer the lake separates into a warm upper layer that floats on a cold lower layer. Which statement about water explains why the layers sit in that order?

choices.text: Above about 4 °C, warmer water is less dense than colder water.
Above about 4 °C, warmer water is always denser than colder water.
Water density does not change with temperature.
Dissolved oxygen makes the lower layer lighter than the upper one.

why.A: Correct — the less dense warm water rides on top, which is what keeps the cold layer sealed below through the summer.
why.B: If warm water were denser it would sink, and the lake would not layer in the order described.
why.C: If density were unaffected by temperature, nothing would drive the separation in the first place.
why.D: Dissolved gases are present in far too small a quantity to order the layers, and the deep layer is the one that loses oxygen.

context: According to Figure 1, the absorbance of the sample exposed at 200 lux after 30 minutes was:

context: A student predicts that a sample exposed at 1600 lux would have an absorbance below 0.12 after 60 minutes. Do the data support the prediction?

choices.text: Yes, because absorbance is 0.12 at 30 minutes and Figure 1 shows it still falling.
Yes, because Table 1 reports the 60-minute value at 1600 lux directly.

choices.text: records absorbance at several times rather than at a single time.
uses a wider range of light intensities than Study 1 does.
holds the samples at a different temperature throughout.

Yes, because Table 1 reports the value at 30 g/L for Species B directly.
No, because 30 g/L was not tested, so nothing can be said about it.
No, because germination in Species B levels off at every step above 20 g/L.

why.B: The table jumps from 20 g/L to 40 g/L. No 30 g/L row exists.

context: Salt in the soil solution makes water uptake harder for a seed because water tends to move:

choices.text: toward the side with more dissolved solute.
toward the side with less dissolved solute.
toward whichever side of the membrane is warmer.
equally in both directions regardless of solute.

why.A: Osmosis moves water across a membrane toward the higher solute concentration. Salty soil pulls against the seed instead of feeding it.
why.B: That reverses osmosis, and would make salty soil easier to draw from rather than harder.
why.C: Temperature affects rate, but the direction of osmotic movement is set by solute concentration.
why.D: Movement is net in one direction whenever the two sides differ, which is what makes the salinity matter.

why.A: A mass divided by a volume is an amount per amount — how much salt is in a given quantity of solution.

why.C: Litres alone would be a volume, and here they are the denominator.
why.D: A rate of change needs time or another varying quantity in the denominator, and there is none here.

context: Based on Table 2, each doubling of epoxy thickness reduces the mass lost, but the size of each reduction:

choices.text: gets smaller as the coating gets thicker.
gets larger as the coating is made thicker.
stays the same at every doubling of thickness.

how the panels were weighed after each exposure.

why.A: The prefix micro- means one millionth, so 1 µm = 0.000001 m. A 160 µm coating is about a sixth of a millimetre.
why.B: One thousandth of a metre is a millimetre.

context: Zinc is commonly used to protect steel because zinc:

choices.text: corrodes in place of the steel beneath it.
is harder than steel and resists scratching.
prevents salt from dissolving in water.
conducts heat away from the steel surface.

why.C: Salt dissolves in the spray regardless of what the panel is coated with.

why.B: 80 is the total rise across the interval, not the rise per degree.
why.C: This divides by 16 rather than by the 4-degree width of the interval.
why.D: 15 is the inland rise per degree from 20 to 24 °C (280 to 340), the next interval along.

context: Warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen than cooler water. This fact makes the pattern in Figure 1 harder on the fish because, as temperature rises, a fish:

choices.text: needs more oxygen at the same time as less is available.
needs less oxygen at the same time as less is available.
needs more oxygen at the same time as more is available.
needs the same oxygen regardless of temperature.

why.A: Both curves climb with temperature, so demand rises. Supply falls at the same time, which is why the squeeze tightens from both directions.
why.B: Figure 1 shows consumption rising, not falling, as the water warms.
why.C: The premise of the question is that warmer water holds less oxygen, so supply is falling.
why.D: Consumption rises to roughly three times its 8 °C value in both populations, so it clearly depends on temperature.

context: Oxygen consumption in Figure 1 is given in milligrams per kilogram per hour. Expressing it this way rather than in milligrams per hour allows a reader to:

choices.text: compare fish of different sizes on the same scale.
convert directly to a percentage of the oxygen available.
read the total oxygen a fish used over 96 hours.
determine the temperature of the water in the tank.

why.A: Dividing by body mass removes size from the number, so a large fish and a small one can be put on the same axis.
why.B: Nothing in the unit refers to how much oxygen the water holds, so no percentage of availability follows from it.
why.C: A total would need the rate multiplied by a duration and by the fish’s mass; the rate alone does not give it.
why.D: Temperature is the other axis, and the unit says nothing about it.

context: Geologist 1 argues that the structure is:

why.A: Geologist 1 opens by naming it an impact crater and argues from shocked quartz.
why.B: The salt dome is Geologist 2’s account.
why.C: The maar is Geologist 3’s account.
why.D: Faults appear in Geologist 2’s argument as an alternative source of quartz deformation, not as the structure itself.

context: Geologists 2 and 3 agree with each other, and disagree with Geologist 1, about:

choices.text: whether shocked quartz can be produced without a meteorite impact.
whether a thick salt layer underlies the basin at depth.
whether the structure is roughly circular in outline.
whether magma ever reached shallow depths beneath the floor of the basin.

why.A: Geologist 2 offers rapid fault movement and Geologist 3 offers a steam explosion, both as terrestrial sources of the deformation Geologist 1 says only impact can cause.
why.B: Only Geologist 2 builds an argument on the salt layer; Geologist 3 never mentions it.
why.C: All three accept the circular shape and each explains how their process produces it.
why.D: The dikes are Geologist 3’s evidence alone, and Geologist 2 does not address them.

context: The absence of meteorite fragments, given in Table 1 as zero recovered, is used by:

choices.text: Geologists 2 and 3 as evidence against an impact origin.
Geologist 1 as evidence that the impactor vaporised.
all three geologists as their central piece of evidence.
Geologist 3 alone, to argue for a salt origin.

why.A: Geologist 2 states it outright, and Geologist 3 makes a point of the maar leaving no fragments because no meteorite was involved. Geologist 1 never raises the fragments at all.
why.B: Geologist 1 argues only from the shocked quartz and the shape, and says nothing about the impactor’s fate.
why.C: Geologist 1’s case rests on planar deformation features, not on what is missing.
why.D: The salt origin is Geologist 2’s position, not Geologist 3’s.

context: A laboratory finds that rapid movement along a fault produces planar deformation features indistinguishable from those at the site. This finding would most strengthen:

why.A: Geologist 2 specifically proposes fault movement as the alternative source of the planar features, and this supplies the evidence that proposal was missing.
why.B: It weakens Geologist 1, whose argument depends on impact being the only way to reach those pressures.
why.C: Geologist 3 attributes the deformation to a steam explosion, which the finding neither supports nor addresses.
why.D: It bears directly on the one point every position has to account for, so it cannot be neutral.

context: Which finding would most weaken Geologist 2’s position?

choices.text: Drilling shows the salt layer beneath the site is intact and undissolved.
Drilling confirms that the salt layer lies about 1.8 km below the drilling site.
The rim is found to stand 60 m above the level of the flat surrounding plain.
No meteorite fragments are found after a further search.

why.A: Geologist 2’s mechanism requires the salt to have dissolved so the dome above it could collapse. An intact salt layer removes the cause of the collapse.
why.B: Confirming the salt layer is present supports that account rather than weakening it.
why.C: The rim height is already in Table 1 and every position explains it.
why.D: The absence of fragments is evidence Geologist 2 already cites in support.

context: Geologist 3’s argument depends on a claim that Table 1 supports only indirectly, namely that:

choices.text: magma reached shallow depths in this basin.
the structure is approximately 4 km across.
shocked quartz is present in the rim.
no meteorite fragments have been recovered.

why.A: The nearest exposed dike is 9 km away, which shows magma nearby but not under the structure itself. The table gives the distance and leaves the inference to be made.
why.B: The diameter is stated directly in Table 1.
why.C: The shocked quartz count is stated directly, at 12 grains per 100.
why.D: The zero fragment count is stated directly as well.

context: All three geologists would agree that:

choices.text: the structure was formed by a process that excavated or deformed rock in a roughly circular pattern.
shocked quartz needs pressures above 5 gigapascals, which in nature are reachable only by an impact event.
a salt layer is responsible for the raised rim of the structure.
magma played some part in forming the structure at depth.

why.A: Impact, dome collapse and steam explosion are different processes, but each is offered as an account of the same circular structure with its raised rim.
why.B: That threshold is Geologist 1’s premise, and the other two argue the features can form at lower pressures by other routes.
why.C: Only Geologist 2 involves salt.
why.D: Only Geologist 3 involves magma.

context: According to Table 1, the number of shocked quartz grains per 100 sampled was:

why.A: Read the shocked quartz row of Table 1.
why.B: 0 is the count of meteorite fragments recovered.
why.C: 60 is the rim height in metres.
why.D: 9 is the distance in kilometres to the nearest exposed dike.

context: Suppose a crater of confirmed impact origin elsewhere is found to contain 40 shocked quartz grains per 100 sampled. How would this bear on Geologist 1’s position?

choices.text: It would weaken it slightly, since the Saarat count of 12 is well below the confirmed impact figure.
It would strengthen it, since both sites contain shocked quartz.
It would have no bearing, since the two sites lie in different basins.
It would weaken it decisively, since any difference in grain count rules out an impact origin altogether.

why.A: A much lower count at Saarat is a point of difference from a confirmed impact site, which counts against the identification without settling it — concentration could vary with sampling depth or target rock.
why.B: Presence at both sites is common ground; the comparison here is about how much, and Saarat has less than a third as much.
why.C: The whole point of a confirmed case is to give the disputed one something to be measured against.
why.D: "Decisively" overstates it. One comparison site does not establish what range of counts an impact can produce.

context: Geologist 2 states that salt rises through denser overlying rock. The property of salt that makes this possible is its:

choices.text: lower density than the rock above it.
higher melting point than the rock above it.
greater hardness than the rock above it.

why.A: A less dense material under a denser one is buoyant, and over geological time it flows upward through it. That is the mechanism the argument names.
why.B: Melting is not involved; the salt moves as a solid that deforms slowly.
why.C: Hardness would resist deformation, which is the opposite of what rising requires.
why.D: Solubility explains the later collapse in Geologist 2’s account, not the initial rise.

context: Table 1 reports the depth of the salt layer in kilometres and the rim height in metres. The rim height, expressed in kilometres, is:

why.A: There are 1,000 metres in a kilometre, so 60 m is 60/1000 = 0.060 km.
why.B: This divides by 100 rather than by 1,000.
why.C: Dividing by 10 gives this, but a kilometre is a thousand metres, not ten.
why.D: This multiplies by 1,000, which converts in the wrong direction.

context: Which piece of evidence, if found, would be consistent with Geologist 1’s position and inconsistent with both of the others?

choices.text: A layer of iridium-rich sediment of the same age, spread evenly around it.
A ring of upturned sedimentary beds all the way around the rim.
Steam-altered minerals scattered through the rim debris.
A fault trace passing directly beneath the structure and continuing well beyond its raised rim.

why.A: Iridium is rare in the Earth’s crust and abundant in meteorites, so a spread of it dated to the event points at material arriving from outside — which neither a salt collapse nor a steam explosion supplies.
why.B: Upturned beds form at the rim of any structure that was pushed up or blown out, so all three accounts predict them.
why.C: Steam alteration is what Geologist 3’s maar would produce, so it favours that position rather than Geologist 1’s.
why.D: A fault beneath the site is what Geologist 2 needs for the alternative source of deformation.

context: A student asks whether the period would still be independent of bob mass if the pendulum were released from 45°. Based on Experiments 1–3, this question:

choices.text: cannot be answered, because no trial varied the mass at any angle other than 10°.
can be answered yes, because Trial 13 released the pendulum from 45°.
can be answered no, because the period at 45° differs from the period at 10°.
can be answered yes, because Experiment 2 varied the mass across four trials.

why.A: Correct — Experiment 2 varied mass only at 10°, and Experiment 3 varied angle only at 100 g, so the combination was never tested.
why.B: Trial 13 does use 45°, but it holds the mass at 100 g, so it says nothing about whether mass matters there.
why.C: The period does rise at 45°, but that is the effect of the angle, not evidence about the effect of mass at that angle.
why.D: Experiment 2 varied mass at a single release angle of 10°, so its result cannot be carried over to 45°.

context: Based on Table 1 alone, which species would germinate best in soil at 60% moisture?

choices.text: Species A, whose count was the highest of the three at 40% moisture.
Species B, which germinated best at the lowest moisture level tested.
Species C, whose count was still rising at the highest level tested.
It cannot be determined, because 60% lies beyond the range that was tested.

why.A: Species A peaks at 40% and falls by 50%, so its own trend argues against it, and 60% is outside the table anyway.
why.B: Species B peaks at 30% and has fallen to 29 seeds by 50%, the steepest decline of the three.
why.C: Species C is the tempting choice, but a count still rising at the last point tested is not evidence about a level past it.
why.D: Correct — the table stops at 50%, and two of the three species have already turned downward, so nothing in it fixes what happens at 60%.

context: For Species B, the moisture level with the greatest germination and the level with the greatest shoot height are, respectively:

why.A: Correct — Species B germinates best at 30% (88 seeds) and grows tallest at 30% as well (41 mm).
why.B: At 40% Species B falls to 61 seeds and 30 mm, below its values at 30% in both of the tables.
why.C: The germination figure is right, but shoot height peaks at 30% too, not at 40%.
why.D: Both halves are wrong: 40% is the peak for neither measure in Species B.

context: Do the results show whether sand would still take in water fastest if all three soils had begun the test wetter than they did?

choices.text: Yes, because Table 1 reports cumulative infiltration at five separate times.
Yes, because the three soils were tested on the same morning at one station.
No, because every soil was tested at the same single starting water content.
No, because Table 3 reports a rate rather than a cumulative depth of water.

why.A: Repeated readings during one test show how infiltration changes with time, not how it would change with a wetter start.
why.B: Testing all three at one time and place is what makes the comparison fair; it does not extend the result to other conditions.
why.C: Correct — starting water content was held fixed, so the experiment has no trial at a wetter start to compare against.
why.D: Table 3 does report a rate, but rates and depths are interchangeable here; the missing piece is a second starting condition.

context: Across the three soils in Table 2, as clay content increases, bulk density:

why.A: Correct — clay content runs 4% → 19% → 52% while bulk density runs 1.55 → 1.32 → 1.41 g/cm³.
why.B: Bulk density falls from sand to loam before rising again, so it does not climb throughout.
why.C: Bulk density falls only over the first step; the clay soil is denser than the loam.
why.D: This reverses the order: the fall comes first and the rise second.

context: Which property in Table 2 changes in step with the final-interval infiltration rates in Table 3 across all three soils?

choices.text: Clay content, which rises as the infiltration rate falls.
Bulk density, which rises as the infiltration rate falls.
Organic matter, which rises as the infiltration rate falls.
None of the three, since each one varies independently of rate.

why.A: Correct — clay content runs 4% → 19% → 52% as the rate runs 180 → 66 → 18 mm/hr, a clean inverse order.
why.B: Bulk density runs 1.55 → 1.32 → 1.41, which is not in order with the falling rates.
why.C: Organic matter runs 0.8 → 3.6 → 2.1, rising and then falling while the rate only falls.
why.D: One property does track the rate across all three soils, so this goes too far.

context: Do the three studies establish that these cuttings had more stomata on their lower leaf surfaces than on their upper surfaces?

choices.text: Yes, because Study 3 counted the pores on each surface separately.
Yes, because Study 2 showed water loss falling as leaves were removed.
No, because no stomata were counted, though Study 3 is consistent with it.
No, because Study 3 shows the upper surfaces losing the most water.

why.A: Study 3 coated surfaces and weighed the tubes; at no point were pores counted on either surface.
why.B: Study 2 compares whole leaves against one another and never distinguishes the two surfaces of a leaf.
why.C: Correct — coating the lower surfaces cuts loss far more than coating the upper ones, which fits the claim without measuring it.
why.D: Study 3 shows the reverse: coating the lower surfaces produced much the larger reduction.

context: Which pair of conditions in Table 1 differ in the lamp alone, and so isolate the effect of light on water loss?

choices.text: Still air with the lamp on and still air in the dark.
Still air with the lamp on and moving air with the lamp on.
Moving air with the lamp on and still air in the dark.
The humid chamber with the lamp on and still air in the dark.

why.A: Correct — both are still air, so the drop from 1.40 g to 0.60 g can only be the lamp being switched off.
why.B: Both of these have the lamp on; what changes between them is the air movement.
why.C: These differ in two ways at once, in air movement and in light, so neither effect is isolated.
why.D: These differ in humidity and in light together, so the 0.45 g and 0.60 g cannot be attributed to either alone.

context: In Experiment 1, the cycles to first crack for an 18% porosity core is closest to what fraction of the figure for a 4% core?

why.A: Correct — 30 cycles against 210 cycles is 30/210, which reduces to about one seventh.
why.B: One quarter of 210 would be about 53 cycles, well above the 30 recorded at 18% porosity.
why.C: One third of 210 is 70 cycles, close to the 65 recorded for the 12% core rather than the 30 for the 18% core.
why.D: Two thirds of 210 is 140 cycles, close to the 8% figure and more than four times the right value.

context: Which comparison isolates the role of water in the cracking, holding everything else constant?

choices.text: Experiment 2 against Experiment 3 at the same minimum temperature.
Experiment 1 against Experiment 2 at the same core porosity.
The 4% core against the 18% core within Experiment 1 alone.
The −2 °C row against the −20 °C row within Experiment 3 alone.

why.A: Correct — both use 12% porosity cores cycled to the same minimum, and only the soaking differs between them.
why.B: These differ in the minimum temperature as well, since Experiment 1 held it at −10 °C throughout.
why.C: Both of these cores were soaked, so the comparison shows the effect of porosity, not of water.
why.D: Both of these cores were dried, so neither one has water in its pores to begin with.

context: In Trial 1 of Experiment 1 the tray lost 2.0 mm of depth. Over a water surface of 0.50 m², this depth corresponds to a volume closest to:

why.A: Correct — 2.0 mm is 0.0020 m, and 0.0020 m × 0.50 m² is 0.0010 m³, which is 1.0 L.
why.B: 0.10 L is a tenth of the volume; the metre-to-millimetre conversion has slipped a factor of ten.
why.C: 10 L would need a depth of 20 mm, half the water the tray was filled with.
why.D: 4.0 L multiplies 2.0 by 2 instead of by the 0.50 m² surface the water sits on.

context: The shade-cloth tray in Experiment 2 lost 620 g of water. Taking 1.00 g of water to occupy 1.00 mL, this mass corresponds to a volume of:

why.A: 0.0620 L is 62 mL, a tenth of the mass the tray actually lost.
why.B: 6.20 L is ten times too large; 620 mL is well under one litre, not over six.
why.C: Correct — 620 g of water is 620 mL, and 620 mL is 0.620 L.
why.D: 62.0 L is a hundred times the volume, and the tray holds only 20 L in total.

context: At 25 °C the tray in Experiment 3 lost water at 60 mL/h. If that rate held for a full 24 hours, the volume lost would be closest to:

why.A: 0.144 L is 144 mL, which is the loss over about two and a half hours.
why.B: 2.50 L divides 60 by 24 rather than multiplying, then treats the result as litres.
why.C: 14.4 L is ten times too large; 1440 mL is 1.44 L, not 14.4 L.
why.D: Correct — 60 mL/h × 24 h is 1440 mL, and 1440 mL is 1.44 L.

context: According to Table 1, the rate of water loss first reaches twice its still-air value at a wind speed of:

why.A: Correct — still air loses 2.0 mm/day, and 2.0 m/s is the first trial to reach 4.0 mm/day.
why.B: At 4.0 m/s the loss is four times the still-air value, so the doubling happened earlier.
why.C: No trial ran at 8.0 m/s, and the loss had already doubled by 2.0 m/s in any case.
why.D: At 1.0 m/s the loss is 3.0 mm/day, which is one and a half times the still-air value.

context: In Table 3, the increase in evaporation rate across each 5 °C step is:

choices.text: the same size at every step.

why.A: Correct — the steps are 9, 13 and 18 mL/h, so the last one is the largest of the three.
why.B: Equal steps would mean a straight-line relationship, but the three increases differ.
why.C: The first step is 20 to 29 mL/h, an increase of 9, which is the smallest of the three.
why.D: The rate climbs from 42 to 60 mL/h above 20 °C, which is the largest increase in the table.

context: According to Table 2, which cover or covers reduced the 24-hour loss to less than one third of the uncovered tray?

choices.text: None of the three covers tested.
The shade cloth, and none of the other covers.
The floating balls and the sealed lid.
The sealed lid and nothing else.

why.A: Two of the covers fall below 333 g, so at least one cover does qualify.
why.B: The shade cloth lost 620 g, which is well over a third of the uncovered 1000 g.
why.C: Correct — a third of 1000 g is about 333 g, and the balls lost 250 g and the lid 15 g.
why.D: The sealed lid qualifies, but so do the floating balls at 250 g.

context: A tray is held at a wind speed of 2.0 m/s for 3 days at 20 °C. Based on Table 1, the total depth of water it loses would be closest to:

why.A: 4 mm is the loss for a single day, not for the three days the question asks about.
why.B: 24 mm uses the 8.0 mm/day figure, which belongs to the 4.0 m/s trial.
why.C: Correct — Table 1 gives 4.0 mm/day at 2.0 m/s, and three days at that rate is 12 mm.
why.D: 6 mm would follow from the still-air rate of 2.0 mm/day rather than the 2.0 m/s rate.

context: Based on Table 3, the evaporation rate of a tray held at 22.5 °C would most likely be closest to:

why.A: 42 mL/h is the rate at 20 °C, and the rate rises with every temperature step in the table.
why.B: 60 mL/h is the rate at 25 °C, which is above the temperature the question names.
why.C: 35 mL/h falls between the 15 °C and 20 °C rows, below the range the question asks about.
why.D: Correct — 22.5 °C sits halfway between 20 and 25 °C, whose rates are 42 and 60 mL/h.

context: A student hypothesised that a cover reduces evaporation only by blocking sunlight from the water. Do the Experiment 2 results support that hypothesis?

choices.text: No, because two covers that both block light gave very different results.
Yes, because every one of the three covers reduced the mass lost.
No, because the shade-cloth tray lost more water than the uncovered tray.
Yes, because the cover that blocked the most light lost the least water.

why.A: Correct — blocking light alone cannot explain a gap between 250 g and 15 g among covers that all shade the water.
why.B: A reduction under every cover is consistent with several explanations, not only with shading.
why.C: The shade-cloth tray lost 620 g against 1000 g uncovered, so it lost less, not more.
why.D: The sealed lid blocks air as well as light, so its result cannot single out shading.

context: On the basis of Experiments 1 and 3 together, the evaporation rate of a tray held at 25 °C in a 4.0 m/s wind:

choices.text: is the sum of those two values once they are in common units.
cannot be determined, because no trial combined warm water with wind.
is 8.0 mm/day, which is exactly the value Table 1 gives for a 4.0 m/s wind.
is 60 mL/h, which is exactly the value Table 3 gives for water at 25 °C.

why.A: Nothing in the two experiments shows that the two effects simply add, and neither was tested with the other.
why.B: Correct — Experiment 1 varied wind at 20 °C and Experiment 3 varied temperature in still air, so the combination was never tested.
why.C: That figure was measured at 20 °C, and the question raises the temperature above it.
why.D: That figure was measured in still air, and the question puts the tray in a 4.0 m/s wind.

context: Evaporation cools the water that stays behind in the tray. This happens chiefly because the molecules that escape the surface:

choices.text: release heat into the water as they enter the gas phase.
reduce the surface area available for further evaporation.
carry away more than the average kinetic energy of the water.
leave behind molecules that are moving faster on average.

why.A: Entering the gas phase absorbs energy from the water; it does not release heat into it.
why.B: The surface area of the tray is fixed by its shape and does not change as water leaves.
why.C: Correct — only the fastest molecules escape, so the average energy of what remains falls.
why.D: Losing the fastest molecules lowers the average speed of those left, rather than raising it.

context: Moving air increases evaporation from an open surface. The best explanation for this effect is that wind:

choices.text: raises the temperature of the water at the surface of the tray.
increases the atmospheric pressure pushing down on the water’s surface.
adds kinetic energy directly to the molecules in the liquid.
carries away humid air before it can slow further evaporation.

why.A: Moving air usually cools an evaporating surface rather than warming it.
why.B: Wind does not raise atmospheric pressure, and higher pressure would slow evaporation anyway.
why.C: Wind acts on the air above the surface; it does not push energy into the liquid below.
why.D: Correct — still air above the water grows humid, and a humid layer returns molecules as fast as it loses them.

context: Trial 1 of Experiment 1 and the uncovered tray of Experiment 2 were run under the same conditions. Which calculation shows that the two results agree?

choices.text: 2.0 mm across 0.50 m² is 1.0 L of water, which has a mass of 1000 g.
2.0 mm across 0.50 m² is 100 mL of water, which has a mass of 1000 g.
2.0 mm across 0.50 m² is 1.0 L of water, which has a mass of 100 g.
2.0 mm across 0.50 m² is 2.0 L of water, which has a mass of 1000 g.

why.A: Correct — 0.002 m × 0.50 m² is 0.001 m³, which is one litre and so one thousand grams.
why.B: One litre is 1000 mL, so calling the same volume 100 mL is off by a factor of ten.
why.C: A litre of water has a mass of 1000 g rather than 100 g, so the trials would not match.
why.D: The volume works out to 0.001 m³, which is 1.0 L; doubling it breaks the agreement.

context: A district wants the Table 3 result for 25 °C expressed as a depth of water lost per day from a tray of 0.50 m². That depth is closest to:

why.A: That would follow from using twelve hours rather than the full day the question names.
why.B: Correct — 60 mL/h over 24 h is 1440 cm³, and 1440 cm³ spread over 5000 cm² is 0.29 cm.
why.C: That is the depth in centimetres rather than millimetres, so it is ten times too small.
why.D: Using 500 cm² instead of 5000 cm² for the tray makes the depth ten times too large.

context: Table 3 reports an infiltration rate for sand of 180 mm/hr. That figure follows from Table 1 because sand takes in:

choices.text: 130 mm in the first 20 minutes, which is 180 mm in an hour.
80 mm in the first 10 minutes, which is 180 mm in an hour.
60 mm between 20 and 40 minutes, which is 180 mm in an hour.
190 mm over the 40 minutes, which is 180 mm in an hour.

why.A: The first twenty minutes run faster than the last and work out near 390 mm/hr.
why.B: Ten minutes of cumulative depth gives about 480 mm/hr, far above the reported rate.
why.C: Correct — 190 − 130 is 60 mm across a twenty-minute interval, and 60 × 3 is 180.
why.D: Averaging the whole test folds in the fast early minutes and gives about 285 mm/hr.

context: Table 2 gives loam a bulk density of 1.32 g/cm³. Expressed in kilograms per cubic metre, that density is:

why.A: That is ten times too small, as though a cubic metre held only 100,000 cm³.
why.B: That is ten times too large and would make loam denser than most solid rock.
why.C: Keeping the number unchanged ignores both conversions: 1 kg is 1000 g and 1 m³ is 1,000,000 cm³, so the value must be multiplied by 1000.
why.D: Correct — a cubic metre holds 1,000,000 cm³, so it holds 1,320,000 g of loam, which is 1320 kg; the density is 1320 kg/m³.

context: Across Table 1, the way depth lost responds to wind changes above 2.0 m/s: each further 1.0 m/s of wind then costs:

choices.text: twice as much depth as it did below 2.0 m/s.
half as much depth as it did below 2.0 m/s.
the same depth as it did below 2.0 m/s.
no further depth once 4.0 mm has been lost.

why.A: Correct — 1.0 mm per m/s up to 2.0 m/s, then 4.0 mm across the next 2.0 m/s.
why.B: Halving would put the 4.0 m/s trial near 5.0 mm rather than at the 8.0 mm recorded.
why.C: A steady rate would put the 4.0 m/s trial at 6.0 mm, which is not what Table 1 shows.
why.D: Depth lost keeps climbing past 4.0 mm, reaching 8.0 mm at the highest wind speed.

context: Suppose a tray covered with floating balls were run in the wind tunnel at 2.0 m/s for 24 hours. Based on all three tables, the mass of water lost would be closest to:

choices.text: 2000 g, the loss an uncovered tray shows at that wind speed.
500 g, a quarter of what an uncovered tray loses at that wind speed.
250 g, the same loss the floating balls allowed in still air.
1000 g, the loss an uncovered tray shows in still air.

why.A: That is the uncovered loss at that wind speed, with the cover not applied at all.
why.B: Correct — 4.0 mm is 2000 g uncovered, and floating balls leave about a quarter of that.
why.C: The still-air figure takes no account of the wind, which doubles the uncovered loss.
why.D: That is what an uncovered tray loses before either the wind or the cover is applied.

context: A fourth soil, tested in the same way, has a clay content of about 30%. If clay content orders it among the other soils as it does in Tables 2 and 3, its final-interval infiltration rate would most likely be:

why.A: Correct — 30% clay lies between loam’s 19% and clay’s 52% in Table 2, so its rate should fall between their Table 3 rates of 66 and 18 mm/hr.
why.B: A rate below 18 mm/hr belongs to a soil with more clay than the 52% of the clay soil, not less.
why.C: That range sits between sand and loam, which hold only 4% and 19% clay.
why.D: Only a soil with less clay than sand’s 4% would be expected to beat sand’s 180 mm/hr.

context: Between the first 5 minutes of a test and the final 20 minutes, the infiltration rate falls by the largest factor for:

choices.text: loam, which falls further than either other soil.
sand, which falls further than either other soil.
all three, whose rates fall by the same factor.
clay, whose rate falls by a factor of about four.

why.A: Loam falls from roughly 240 to 66 mm/hr, a factor near 3.6 rather than the largest.
