smaller, so the face lies closer to horizontal.
exactly 30 degrees, which was the best angle found in Table 1.

why.A: Table 1 shows output changing by more than 40 W across the tilts tested, so the angle plainly matters.
why.B: Correct. A low sun arrives at a shallow angle, and standing the face up further is what turns it to meet that light head on.
why.C: Lying the face flat points it at the overhead sky, which is what suits a high sun rather than a low one.
why.D: Table 1 was taken at one site on one day; 30 degrees is the best angle for those conditions, not everywhere.

context: Based on Table 2, the output of the panel at a cell temperature of 50 degrees C would most likely be closest to:

why.A: Correct. 50 degrees C sits midway between the 45 degree reading of 146 W and the 55 degree reading of 139 W.
why.B: This lies above the 45 degree C reading, but 50 degrees C is warmer than 45, so output should be lower.
why.C: This is the reading at 65 degrees C, three steps warmer than the temperature asked about.
why.D: This falls below the 55 degree C reading of 139 W, but 50 degrees C is cooler than 55, so output should be higher.

context: Which of the following is the largest output reported anywhere in Tables 1, 2 and 3?

why.A: 146 W is the freshly cleaned reading in Table 3 and the 45 degree C reading in Table 2.
why.B: 156 W is the 45 degree tilt reading, which is the second highest in Table 1 alone.
why.C: Correct. 159 W appears at a tilt of 30 degrees in Table 1 and at 25 degrees C in Table 2, and nothing in any table beats it.
why.D: 132 W is the flat-panel reading in Table 1 and the smallest of these four.

context: According to Table 1, which antibiotic produced the largest zone of inhibition on Strain A?

why.A: W produced the smallest zone in Table 1, at 9 mm, which is below the 15 mm the laboratory treats as susceptible.
why.B: X produced 14 mm, larger than W but smaller than both Y and Z.
why.C: Correct. Y produced 22 mm, the largest zone in Table 1.
why.D: Z produced 18 mm, which is the second largest zone rather than the largest.

context: In Experiment 1, which of the following was the same for all four discs tested?

choices.text: The identity of the antibiotic used.
The mass of antibiotic on the disc.
The bacterial strain the discs were laid on, but not the growing time.

why.A: The four discs carried four different antibiotics, W, X, Y and Z; that is the variable being changed.
why.B: Correct. Experiment 1 loaded every disc at 10 micrograms, which is what makes the four zones comparable.
why.C: The zones ranged from 9 mm to 22 mm, and that spread is the result the experiment was run to find.
why.D: The strain was indeed the same, but so was the growing time; the passage fixes 18 hours at 35 degrees C for every test.

context: According to Table 2, a zone of 27 mm was produced by a disc carrying how much Antibiotic Y?

why.A: Correct. The 30 microgram row of Table 2 gives a zone of 27 mm.
why.B: 100 micrograms produced the largest zone in Table 2, at 32 mm.
why.C: 3 micrograms produced a 16 mm zone, only just over the 15 mm susceptibility mark.
why.D: 10 micrograms produced 22 mm, which is the reading Table 1 also reports for Y.

context: One test appears in both Table 1 and Table 2. Comparing the two tables, that shared test:

choices.text: gives 22 mm in Table 1 and 11 mm in Table 2.
gives 14 mm in both, so the two experiments agree.
appears only in Table 1, since Table 2 used a different strain.
gives 22 mm in both, so the two experiments agree.

why.A: 11 mm is the Strain C reading for Y in Table 3, not anything reported in Table 2.
why.B: 14 mm belongs to Antibiotic X in Table 1 and appears nowhere in Table 2.
why.C: Experiment 2 used Strain A, the same strain as Experiment 1; it was Experiment 3 that changed the strain.
why.D: Correct. Antibiotic Y at 10 micrograms on Strain A gives 22 mm in Table 1 and 22 mm in Table 2, exactly as the passage says it should.

context: In Table 2, each threefold increase in the mass on the disc adds roughly 5 mm to the zone. On that pattern, a disc carrying 300 micrograms of Antibiotic Y on Strain A would give a zone closest to:

why.A: 27 mm is the 30 microgram reading, a tenfold smaller dose than the one asked about.
why.B: 32 mm is the 100 microgram reading, the starting point rather than the answer.
why.C: Correct. 300 micrograms is one threefold step above 100 micrograms, so add about 5 mm to the 32 mm reading.
why.D: This multiplies the zone by three along with the dose, but the table shows zones growing by a fixed few millimetres, not in proportion.

context: Using the laboratory 15 mm mark, Strain C would be classed as susceptible to which antibiotic or antibiotics at 10 micrograms?

why.A: Z reaches 17 mm, so at least one antibiotic clears the threshold.
why.B: Correct. In Table 3 only Z clears 15 mm, at 17 mm; W, X and Y give 0, 7 and 11 mm.
why.C: Y gives 11 mm on Strain C, which is four millimetres short of the mark even though it was the best performer on Strain A.
why.D: X gives only 7 mm on Strain C, less than half the mark.

context: Comparing Table 1 with Table 3, which antibiotic lost the most zone diameter when the strain was changed from A to C?

why.A: Correct. Y fell from 22 mm to 11 mm, a loss of 11 mm, larger than any other antibiotic here.
why.B: Z fell from 18 mm to 17 mm, a loss of just 1 mm, the smallest of the four.
why.C: W fell from 9 mm to 0 mm, a loss of 9 mm — the most complete failure, but not the largest loss in millimetres.
why.D: X fell from 14 mm to 7 mm, a loss of 7 mm.

context: Experiment 3 used the same four antibiotics at the same 10 micrograms as Experiment 1. This was done primarily so that:

choices.text: the effect of changing the dose on zone size could be measured.
the zones on Strain C would all be larger than those on Strain A.
the growing time could be shortened for the second strain.
any difference in zone size could be attributed to the strain.

why.A: That is what Experiment 2 does, by varying the mass of a single antibiotic; Experiment 3 holds mass fixed.
why.B: Every zone on Strain C was smaller than the matching zone on Strain A, and in any case an experiment is not run to guarantee a result.
why.C: The passage states that every test in all three experiments ran for the same 18 hours at 35 degrees C.
why.D: Correct. Holding the antibiotics and the dose fixed leaves the strain as the only thing that changed between the two tables.

context: The largest disc in Table 2 carried 100 micrograms of Antibiotic Y. Expressed in milligrams, that mass is:

why.A: Correct. There are 1,000 micrograms in a milligram, so 100 micrograms is one tenth of a milligram.
why.B: A full milligram would be 1,000 micrograms, ten times the mass on the disc.
why.C: 10 mg would be 10,000 micrograms, a hundred times the mass on the disc.
why.D: This multiplies by a thousand instead of dividing, turning a speck of powder into a mass of about 100 grams.

context: Suppose Antibiotic Y on Strain C gains about 5 mm of zone for each threefold increase in dose, as it does on Strain A. Starting from the Table 3 reading, the smallest dose listed in Table 2 that would bring Strain C to the 15 mm mark is:

why.A: 100 micrograms would clear the mark too, at roughly 21 mm, but it is not the smallest listed dose that does so.
why.B: 1 microgram is two threefold steps below the 10 microgram reading, so the zone would shrink rather than grow toward 15 mm.
why.C: 3 micrograms is one threefold step below 10 micrograms, so the zone would shrink to about 6 mm rather than grow.
why.D: Correct. Strain C gives 11 mm at 10 micrograms, and one threefold step up to 30 micrograms adds about 5 mm, reaching roughly 16 mm.

context: A student proposes that zone diameter measures only how quickly an antibiotic spreads through the jelly, and not how strongly it stops bacteria. Which result is hardest for that proposal to explain?

choices.text: Every zone measured includes the 6 mm width of the disc itself.
Strain C had come from a patient who had previously been treated with Antibiotic W.
One antibiotic gave five different zones at five different doses on one strain.
Four different antibiotics gave four different zones in Experiment 1.

why.A: That is a constant added to every measurement and so cannot distinguish between any two explanations of the differences.
why.B: This bears on why W failed on Strain C, not on what a zone diameter is measuring.
why.C: Correct. Table 2 changes the amount of one molecule, whose spreading speed does not change with dose, and the zone still moves from 11 mm to 32 mm.
why.D: Four different molecules could easily spread at four different speeds, so this result fits the proposal rather than straining it.

context: Antibiotics act on bacteria and have no effect on viruses. The method described in this passage would therefore be unsuitable for testing a treatment for:

why.A: Strep throat is caused by a bacterium and would grow the lawn this method requires.
why.B: Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium, so a disc test of this kind is possible in principle.
why.C: Food poisoning of this sort is bacterial, and plating the organism is a standard way to test it.
why.D: Correct. Influenza is caused by a virus, which would not form the bacterial lawn the method depends on.

context: Scientist 1 claims that the collapse of the colony was caused primarily by:

choices.text: a shortage of sand eels to feed the chicks.
the arrival of rats on the island.
an increase in severe autumn storms.
competition from the colony on Fara.

why.A: That is the position of Scientist 2, who points to the sand eel decline beginning in 1985.
why.B: Correct. Scientist 1 opens by naming rats as the cause and argues from their arrival in 1991.
why.C: That is the position of Scientist 3, who notes that severe autumn storms roughly doubled in frequency.
why.D: Fara is mentioned only by Scientist 2, and as a comparison colony rather than a competitor.

context: Scientist 2 argues that the decline began before rats arrived. Which of the following most directly supports that argument?

choices.text: A severe storm flooded the southern terrace in 2004.
The count had fallen below 3,000 pairs by 1990.
Rats were first recorded on the island in 1991.
Fledging success had fallen to 0.21 by 1998.

why.A: A storm in 2004 falls long after the period Scientist 2 is pointing to.
why.B: Correct. A fall of more than a thousand pairs before 1991 is a decline that rats cannot have caused, whatever they did afterwards.
why.C: This establishes when rats arrived but says nothing on its own about what happened before.
why.D: The 1998 figure comes seven years after rats arrived, so it fits the rat account at least as comfortably.

context: Scientist 1 and Scientist 3 disagree most directly about:

choices.text: whether the petrels dig burrows in the soil or nest openly on the surface of the island.
whether landings of sand eels declined in the sea around the island.
what it means that the high northern slope failed at the same rate as the terrace.
whether the count of breeding pairs really fell between 1978 and 2012.

why.A: The introduction states that petrels nest in burrows and under boulders, and no account disputes it.
why.B: The sand eel decline is also given in the introduction, and neither of these two scientists denies it.
why.C: Correct. Scientist 1 reads that fact as clearing storms of blame; Scientist 3 reads it as showing the terrace has been ruined.
why.D: All three accept the counts in the shared introduction, which fall from 4,200 pairs to 190.

context: Suppose burrows on the high northern slope were found to have failed at a much lower rate than burrows on the southern terrace. This finding would most weaken the argument of:

why.A: Scientist 2 argues from food supply at sea and never relies on how the two parts of the island compare.
why.B: This finding would strengthen Scientist 3, since flooding reached the terrace and not the slope.
why.C: The finding bears on where on the island birds failed, which only two of the three accounts turn on, and in opposite directions.
why.D: Correct. Scientist 1 rules out flooding precisely because the high slope failed at the same rate, and this finding removes that step.

context: All three scientists would most likely agree that:

choices.text: the number of breeding pairs at Ard Skerry fell sharply between 1978 and 2012.
rats were present on Ard Skerry before 1985.
flooding destroyed most burrows on the northern slope.
the Fara colony declined at the same rate over the same years.

why.A: Correct. The counts of 4,200, 1,900 and 190 pairs are in the shared introduction, and every account is an attempt to explain them.
why.B: The introduction dates the first record of rats to 1991, and Scientist 2 leans on their absence before then.
why.C: Scientist 3 says the 2004 storm took the southern terrace; the northern slope is the ground it never reached.
why.D: Scientist 2 states that the Fara colony held steady, which is the whole point of raising it.

context: Scientist 2 raises the colony on Fara in order to:

choices.text: explain why fledging success at Ard Skerry was still 0.66 in 1990.
challenge the claim that the presence of rats is enough to cause a collapse.
show that severe storms did not reach that part of the coast.
establish that sand eel landings fell across the whole region, including the waters around Fara.

why.A: The 1990 figure is used to argue that the decline predates the rats, and it is not what the Fara comparison is for.
why.B: Correct. Fara had rats throughout and held steady, which is offered as a case where rats did not produce the outcome Scientist 1 attributes to them.
why.C: Storms are Scientist 3’s subject, and nothing is said about what weather Fara received.
why.D: The point made about Fara is the opposite: its birds fished a different bank, so the food supply there was not the same.

context: Each of the three scientists offers an explanation for why the count kept falling even after the worst years. Which pairing is correct?

choices.text: Scientist 2: burrows that collapse must be dug again in waterlogged ground.
Scientist 3: rats keep taking eggs long after they arrive.
Scientist 1: adults that lose a chick tend to move elsewhere the next year.
Scientist 1: light fledglings rarely return to breed.

why.A: The waterlogged ground argument belongs to Scientist 3, who is explaining the cost of a collapsed burrow.
why.B: Rats are Scientist 1’s subject; Scientist 3 does not appeal to them at all.
why.C: Correct. Scientist 1 closes on exactly this point, offering it as the reason the count kept falling after 1991.
why.D: The light fledgling argument belongs to Scientist 2, not Scientist 1.

context: Fledging success fell from 0.66 in 1990 to 0.21 in 1998. Scientist 1 treats this change as important because it:

choices.text: coincides with the end of the sand eel decline.
occurred entirely after the severe storm of 2004.
shows that fledging success was rising throughout that period.
brackets the year rats were first recorded on the island.

why.A: The introduction dates the sand eel decline to 1985 through 2000, and that is the point Scientist 2 makes rather than Scientist 1.
why.B: Both years fall well before 2004, so the storm cannot be what separates them.
why.C: A fall from 0.66 to 0.21 is a drop of roughly two thirds.
why.D: Correct. Rats were recorded in 1991, which sits between the two years, and Scientist 1 says nothing else does.

context: Which finding, if confirmed, would most strengthen Scientist 2 and weaken both of the others?

choices.text: Chicks that fledged after 1995 weighed markedly less than those that fledged in 1978.
Rat droppings were found inside failed burrows on the southern terrace.
Seawater reached the high northern slope during a storm in 2009.
The 1978 count was later shown to have been an underestimate of the colony's size.

why.A: Correct. Underweight fledglings are the mechanism Scientist 2 proposes, and neither a rat nor a flood leaves a chick alive but light.
why.B: This is direct evidence for Scientist 1 rather than against.
why.C: Seawater reaching the high slope would support Scientist 3 by extending flooding to the ground Scientist 1 treats as safe.
why.D: A larger 1978 figure would make the total decline steeper without favouring any one explanation of it.

context: Scientist 3 accounts for the poor performance of the high northern slope by arguing that it:

choices.text: was where the rats first came ashore when they arrived in 1991.
has always been the poorer ground, being thin turf over rock.
was reached by the 2004 storm along with the terrace.
holds most of the colony and always has.

why.A: The introduction places the grounded boat on the north shore, but Scientist 3 makes no use of rats at all.
why.B: Correct. Scientist 3 says the slope has always been poorer ground, so its failing now does not mean it was ever safe.
why.C: Scientist 3 says the storm took the southern terrace; the slope is the ground it did not reach.
why.D: Scientist 3 says the terrace held most of the colony when the counts began.

context: A fourth researcher proposes that the three causes acted together, each one making the others more costly. This proposal is most consistent with which observation from the shared introduction?

choices.text: A pair lays one egg a year, so the colony can only recover slowly.
Chicks leave the burrow about sixty days after hatching.
The three proposed causes overlap in time across the period of the decline.

why.A: A single egg a year limits how fast any colony can recover, which is true whatever the cause.
why.B: The length of the chick period is the same under every account and does not distinguish between them.
why.C: Correct. The sand eel decline ran from 1985, rats arrived in 1991 and the storms worsened across the same span, so all three were in play at once.
why.D: The final count tells you the outcome was severe, not how many causes produced it.

context: Scientist 2 argues that a colony can keep shrinking even in years when many chicks leave the burrow. This argument depends on the assumption that:

choices.text: rats take adults as readily as they take chicks.
fledging success was recorded accurately only after 1995.
burrows on the terrace flood more often than burrows on the slope.
how well a fledgling is fed affects whether it survives to breed later.

why.A: Scientist 2 attributes nothing to rats and would gain nothing from this claim.
why.B: Scientist 2 relies on the 1978 and 1990 figures, so treating the early record as unreliable would undercut the argument.
why.C: This is a claim about flooding, which belongs to the dispute between Scientists 1 and 3.
why.D: Correct. Without that link, a chick that leaves the burrow is simply a success, and the count would track fledging success rather than drifting below it.

context: According to Table 1, the discharge at a stage of 1.60 m was closest to:

why.A: Correct — Table 1 pairs a stage of 1.60 m with a discharge of 33.5 m cubed/s.
why.B: That is the discharge at the lower stage of 1.20 m.
why.C: That is the discharge at the higher stage of 2.00 m.
why.D: That is the discharge far lower down the curve, at a stage of 0.80 m.

context: According to Table 2, the lowest mean monthly discharge of the year occurred in:

why.A: February is 38.0 m cubed/s, among the highest months of the year.
why.B: Correct — August is 3.8 m cubed/s, below every other month in Table 2.
why.C: July is 4.5 m cubed/s, which is low but not the lowest.
why.D: June is 8.0 m cubed/s, roughly twice the August value.

context: Based on Table 3, as discharge increased from 5 to 85 m cubed/s, suspended sediment concentration:

choices.text: increased and then levelled off above 30 m cubed/s.
decreased throughout, most steeply at the highest discharges.
increased throughout, and by a larger step at each increase.
increased throughout, and by a smaller step at each increase.

why.A: The largest rise of all comes between 55 and 85 m cubed/s, so nothing levels off.
why.B: Every value in the column is larger than the one above it.
why.C: Correct — the steps are 36, 92, 240 and 520 mg/L, each larger than the one before it.
why.D: The steps grow rather than shrink across the five rows.

context: A stage of 1.00 m was recorded. Based on Table 1, the discharge was most likely between:

why.A: That range belongs to stages between 0.40 m and 0.80 m, below the reading given.
why.B: That range belongs to stages between 1.20 m and 1.60 m, above the reading given.
why.C: That range belongs to stages between 1.60 m and 2.00 m, well above the reading given.
why.D: Correct — 1.00 m lies between the tabulated stages of 0.80 m and 1.20 m, whose discharges are 6.5 and 17.0 m cubed/s.

context: Which statement best describes the shape of the rating curve in Table 1?

choices.text: Each equal rise in stage adds more discharge than the rise before it.
Each equal rise in stage adds the same amount of discharge.
Each equal rise in stage adds less discharge than the rise before it.
Discharge rises to a maximum near 1.60 m and then falls away.

why.A: Correct — the stage rises in equal 0.40 m steps while the discharge steps are 5.3, 10.5, 16.5, 22.5 and 29.0 m cubed/s.
why.B: Equal steps would give a straight line, and the increments are not equal.
why.C: The increments grow rather than shrink as the stage rises.
why.D: Discharge is still rising at the top of the table, at 2.40 m.

context: The rating curve was fitted from 14 direct measurements. A stage of 3.20 m is later recorded. Using the curve to obtain a discharge for that stage is questionable mainly because:

choices.text: discharge cannot exceed the highest value that appears in Table 1.
the stage lies beyond the range over which the curve was established.
stage cannot be read accurately when the river is in flood.
the relationship between stage and discharge is known to be a straight line.

why.A: Table 1 lists values at chosen stages; it does not set a ceiling on the river.
why.B: Correct — Table 1 stops at 2.40 m, so 3.20 m asks the curve to predict outside the range the measurements covered.
why.C: The passage says stage is the quantity that is easy to read continuously.
why.D: The table shows a curve that steepens, not a straight line, and a straight line would raise no objection anyway.

context: Based on Table 2, the mean discharge in January exceeded that in July by approximately how many m cubed/s?

why.A: That is the July value on its own, not the excess of January over it.
why.B: That is roughly the ratio of the two months, which is a number of times, not a discharge.
why.C: Correct — 41.0 m cubed/s minus 4.5 m cubed/s is 36.5 m cubed/s.
why.D: That is the sum of the two months rather than the difference between them.

context: Using Table 3 and the relationship given in the passage, the sediment load at a discharge of 85 m cubed/s was closest to:

why.A: This is the right calculation with one factor of ten dropped.
why.B: This is the right calculation with one factor of ten added.
why.C: That is the mass of sediment in a single cubic metre, not the load passing each second.
why.D: Correct — 900 mg/L is 900 000 mg per m cubed, or 0.9 kg per m cubed, and 0.9 kg times 85 m cubed/s is 76.5 kg/s.

context: Which of the following is the best description of discharge as the passage defines it?

choices.text: A volume of water passing a point per unit of time.
The depth of water standing above a fixed reference datum.
The mass of sediment carried in each litre of water.
The total volume of water stored in the catchment.

why.A: Correct — the first paragraph defines it as the volume passing the station each second, in cubic metres per second.
why.B: That is the definition of stage, which the passage distinguishes from discharge.
why.C: That is suspended sediment concentration, defined in the fourth paragraph.
why.D: Nothing in the passage reports a stored volume for the 480 km squared catchment.

context: Between which pair of consecutive months in Table 2 did mean discharge change at the greatest rate?

why.A: That step is 7.0 m cubed/s, large but still less than 8.8.
why.B: Correct — 6.2 to 15.0 m cubed/s is a change of 8.8, the largest single month-to-month step in the table.
why.C: That step is 3.5 m cubed/s, well short of the September-to-October change.
why.D: That step is 3.0 m cubed/s, one of the smaller changes in the table.

context: A student reports the August mean discharge as "3.8 m cubed." The report is incomplete because discharge must be given:

choices.text: as a mass rather than a volume.

why.A: Discharge is defined as a volume; it is the sediment load that is a mass per second.
why.B: A datum is needed for stage, which is a height, not for discharge.
why.C: Correct — discharge is a volume per second, so a bare volume names no flow at all.
why.D: Dividing by area would give a different quantity, and the passage never expresses discharge that way.

context: Based on the passage, a concentration of 140 mg/L is the same as:

why.A: This is ten times too large, as though a cubic metre held 10 000 L.
why.B: This treats milligrams and kilograms as the same unit.
why.C: A litre holds only 140 mg, which is 0.000140 kg, not 0.140 kg.
why.D: Correct — 140 mg/L times 1000 L per m cubed is 140 000 mg per m cubed, and 140 000 mg is 0.140 kg.

context: In Experiment 1, the number of cuttings that rooted at 500 ppm IBA was:

why.A: Correct — Table 1 gives 21 of 30 rooted at 500 ppm.
why.B: That is the untreated group at 0 ppm.
why.C: That is the 1000 ppm group, the best in the experiment.
why.D: That is the 3000 ppm group, which rooted slightly fewer than at 1000 ppm.

context: Based on Table 2, the number rooted was highest at a bench temperature of:

why.A: Eleven rooted at 14 degrees C, the lowest result in Table 2.
why.B: Correct — 27 of 30 rooted at 26 degrees C, one more than at any other temperature tested.
why.C: Twenty-six rooted at 22 degrees C, just below the peak.
why.D: Only 17 rooted at 30 degrees C, a sharp fall from the peak.

context: Which variable was deliberately changed in Experiment 2 but held constant in Experiment 1?

why.A: All cuttings in all three experiments were 18 cm long.
why.B: All cuttings were scored after the same 21 days.
why.C: Correct — Experiment 1 held every tray at 22 degrees C, and Experiment 2 varied the bench temperature across five values.
why.D: IBA was the variable in Experiment 1 and was fixed at 1000 ppm in Experiment 2.

context: The statement that the 1000 ppm group of Experiment 1, the 22 degrees C group of Experiment 2, and the middle group of Experiment 3 were treated identically is important because it:

choices.text: shows that IBA concentration had no effect on the number of cuttings that rooted.
proves that the three experiments were run on the same day.
means that only 30 cuttings in total were used across the study.
lets results from the three experiments be compared against a shared reference point.

why.A: Table 1 shows rooting rising from 9 to 26 as IBA rises, which is a large effect.
why.B: Identical treatment says nothing about when each experiment was carried out.
why.C: Experiment 1 alone used 120 cuttings, in four groups of 30.
why.D: Correct — a condition repeated in all three tables ties them together, and all three report the same 26 of 30.

context: A grower wants to know whether 3000 ppm IBA would still be the poorer choice at 26 degrees C. These experiments cannot answer that because:

choices.text: 3000 ppm was tried only at 22 degrees C.
Experiment 2 did not include a temperature as high as 26 degrees C.
the mean number of roots was not recorded in Experiment 2.
cuttings were scored as rooted at 5 mm rather than at a longer root length.

why.A: Correct — 3000 ppm appears only in Experiment 1, every group of which was held at 22 degrees C.
why.B: Experiment 2 tested 26 degrees C, but only at 1000 ppm.
why.C: A missing root count would not prevent a comparison of numbers rooted.
why.D: The 5 mm threshold was applied uniformly and does not favour either concentration.

context: Which hypothesis is best supported by Table 1 alone?

choices.text: Cuttings will not root at all without an application of IBA.
Rooting improves with IBA up to a point, beyond which more gives no further gain.
Rooting improves steadily with every increase in IBA concentration.
IBA improves the number of roots per cutting but not the number of cuttings that root.

why.A: Nine of the 30 untreated cuttings rooted with no IBA at all.
why.B: Correct — rooting rises from 9 to 21 to 26 and then falls to 24 at the highest concentration.
why.C: The 3000 ppm group did worse than the 1000 ppm group on both measures.
why.D: Both measures rise with IBA, from 9 to 26 rooted and from 3.1 to 7.8 roots.

context: A student predicts that cuttings held at 34 degrees C at 1000 ppm would root better than those at 30 degrees C. Table 2 suggests this prediction is:

choices.text: likely, because warmer benches shorten the time needed to root.
unlikely, because no cuttings at all rooted at temperatures above 26 degrees C.
unlikely, because rooting was already falling sharply above 26 degrees C.
likely, because rooting rose with every one of the temperature increases tested.

why.A: Time to root was not measured; all cuttings were scored at 21 days.
why.B: Seventeen of 30 rooted at 30 degrees C, so rooting had not stopped.
why.C: Correct — the count drops from 27 at 26 degrees C to 17 at 30 degrees C, so the trend is already downward.
why.D: Rooting fell between 26 and 30 degrees C rather than rising throughout.

context: In Experiment 3, how many more tip cuttings than woody base cuttings rooted?

why.A: That is the tip count on its own rather than the difference.
why.B: That is the sum of the two groups.
why.C: That is the difference in mean roots per cutting, not in the number that rooted.
why.D: Correct — 28 tip cuttings rooted against 14 from the woody base, a difference of 14.

context: In Experiment 1, the approximate total number of roots produced by the whole 1000 ppm group was:

why.A: Correct — 26 cuttings rooted, each with a mean of 7.8 roots, and 26 times 7.8 is about 203.
why.B: That multiplies the mean by all 30 cuttings, including the four that never rooted.
why.C: That multiplies the mean by 10 rather than by the number that rooted.
why.D: That is the number of cuttings that rooted, not the number of roots.

context: Expressed as a percentage of the cuttings in its group, rooting in Experiment 3 fell from tip to woody base by approximately:

why.A: Ninety-three per cent is the tip figure itself, and the base group was far from zero.
why.B: Correct — 28 of 30 is about 93 per cent and 14 of 30 is about 47 per cent, a fall of roughly 47 points.
why.C: Fourteen is the fall in the number of cuttings, not in percentage points.
why.D: Halving 93 per cent would give about 47 points of fall, not 50.

context: A concentration of 1000 ppm means that in each million parts of the dip solution there are:

context: All cuttings came from a single parent willow. Compared with seedlings raised from seed, cuttings taken this way are:

more genetically varied, since each cutting grows its own roots.
unable to reproduce sexually once they have been rooted.
genetically identical to the parent plant.

context: Scientist 2 argues that the absence of spoil heaps counts against Scientist 1 because quarrying would:

choices.text: require tools that would have been abandoned at the site.
leave the pits deeper than the nodule band rather than at it.
produce pits of very different sizes from one another.
move a large volume of chalk that has to end up somewhere nearby.

Pollen shows that woodland persisted on the down until 3200 years ago.

why.A: Correct — Scientist 3 says the mound is the root plate and the soil it carried, so a mound of bare chalk rubble is the wrong material.
why.B: That moves the woodland date slightly later and still supports the presence of trees.
why.C: Scientist 3 already treats flakes as ordinary material falling into any open hollow.
why.D: Root plates of different trees would not be expected to leave hollows of one depth.

context: Which single observation is claimed as support by Scientist 2 and left unaddressed by both other scientists?

choices.text: The pits are 2 to 3 m across.
The pit long axes cluster near a mapped joint direction.
Charcoal lies at the base of 3 of the 14 excavated pits.
Flint nodules occur about 0.8 m below the surface.

why.B: Correct — the 040-degree alignment matching a 038-degree joint set is Scientist 2’s central evidence, and neither other account mentions it.
why.C: Scientists 1 and 3 both account for the charcoal.
why.D: The nodule band figures in the accounts of both Scientists 1 and 2.

context: Which prediction follows from Scientist 1’s account but not from Scientist 2’s?

choices.text: The chalk under the pits will be more jointed than elsewhere.
Each pit will be paired with a mound of the same volume.
The flint band will be broken beneath the pits.

why.B: Paired mounds belong to Scientist 3.

context: Suppose charcoal from the base of a pit is dated to 5200 years ago. This would be:

choices.text: consistent with Scientist 3 and a difficulty for Scientist 1.
a difficulty for all three accounts equally.
irrelevant, since charcoal cannot be dated.
consistent with Scientist 1 and a difficulty for Scientist 3.

why.A: The date is older than Scientist 3’s woodland clearance, which is the opposite of helpful.
why.B: Scientist 2 makes no claim about the age of the pits, so the date leaves that account untouched.
why.C: Charcoal is routinely dated, and the passage offers it as excavated evidence.

choices.text: The 9 pits with mounds lack flakes, and the 5 with flakes lack mounds.
Every excavated pit reaches exactly the depth of the nodule band.
All 60 pits share the same alignment near 040 degrees.

why.B: A uniform depth points to one process acting throughout.
why.C: A shared alignment is evidence for one cause across the whole field.
why.D: Absent charcoal removes evidence rather than dividing the pits into groups.

context: Scientist 2’s mechanism depends on rainwater becoming mildly acidic. That acidity comes chiefly from:

choices.text: chalk dust dissolving in the water as it falls.
carbon dioxide dissolving in the water to form carbonic acid.
nitrogen gas dissolving in the water to form nitric acid.
oxygen dissolving in the water to form hydrogen peroxide.

why.A: Chalk is a base; dissolving it would raise the pH rather than lower it.
why.B: Correct — dissolved carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, which is what dissolves limestone and chalk, and Scientist 2 names carbon dioxide directly.
why.C: Atmospheric nitrogen is famously unreactive and does not acidify rain by dissolving.
why.D: Dissolved oxygen does not form hydrogen peroxide in rainfall.

context: Chalk and the flint nodules within it differ in that flint is:

choices.text: a metal ore that was smelted at the pit edge.
a soft material that breaks down before the chalk does.
a silica rock that resists the acid that dissolves the surrounding chalk.
a carbonate rock that dissolves faster than the chalk around it.

why.A: Flint is not an ore and is worked by striking, not by smelting.
why.B: Flint is markedly harder and more durable than the chalk enclosing it.
why.C: Correct — flint is a form of silica, which carbonic acid does not attack, which is why it survives as nodules and can be struck into flakes.
why.D: If flint dissolved faster than chalk there would be no nodule band left to quarry.

context: Of the 14 excavated pits, the observation recorded in the greatest number of them was:

why.A: Flakes were found in 5 of the 14, fewer than the mounds.
why.B: Charcoal was the least common, at 3 of the 14.
why.C: The passage reports the nodule band as a feature of the down, not as a count from the excavations.

Doubling the length doubles it, and doubling the area halves it.
Doubling the length quadruples it, and doubling the area halves it.

context: A student hypothesizes that the lamp filament, like the constantan wire, has the same resistance at every voltage tested. Does Figure 1 support this?

choices.text: Yes, because the filament’s current rises at every single step in voltage.
No; its current rises by less at each step, so its resistance grows.
Yes, because both lines begin at zero.
No, because the filament’s current falls as the applied voltage rises.

why.A: A rising current alone does not show a fixed resistance; the size of each rise matters.
why.B: Correct — a fixed resistance gives a straight line, as for the wire, but the filament’s rises shrink from 250 mA to 50 mA per step.
why.C: Every component carries no current at zero voltage, whatever its resistance does later.
why.D: The filament’s current never falls; it rises from 0 to 620 mA.

context: The filament’s resistance rose as the voltage was raised. The most likely reason is that as more current flowed, the filament:

choices.text: became hotter, and the resistance of a metal rises with its temperature.
cooled, and a cold metal carries current less easily than a warm one.
lost electrons, leaving fewer to carry the current.

why.A: Correct — the passage notes the lamp glows brighter as the voltage rises, and a hotter metal resists current more.
why.B: A glowing filament is heating, not cooling, as the current grows.
why.C: A current passes electrons through a metal without using them up.
why.D: A shorter wire would have less resistance, not more, and filaments do not shrink noticeably as they glow.

why.D: That divides 960 s by 0.50 A instead of multiplying by it.

why.C: That divides the charge by the mass, which gives coulombs per milligram.

choices.text: The 0.20 A and 1.20 A trials of Experiment 2
The 0.05 mol/L and 1.00 mol/L trials of Experiment 3
The 32-minute trial of Experiment 1 and the 0.80 A trial of Experiment 2

why.B: These share a time, so they show the effect of current but not that charge alone is what matters.

context: In the 0.05 mol/L trial, the cathode gained less mass than in the 0.50 mol/L trial, although the same charge passed. The most likely explanation is that in the dilute solution:

choices.text: less current flowed, because a dilute solution conducts poorly.
each copper atom was lighter than in the stronger solution.
part of the charge produced hydrogen gas from the water instead of depositing copper.
the anode gained all the copper that the cathode should have received from the solution.

why.A: The passage fixes the current at 0.50 A in every trial of Experiment 3.
why.B: The mass of a copper atom does not depend on the solution it came from.
why.C: Correct — with few copper ions near the cathode, some of the charge is spent reducing water, so less copper is deposited per coulomb.
why.D: Copper leaves the anode during electrolysis; the anode loses mass rather than gaining it.

context: According to Scientist 2, Kelm-7 dims because:

choices.text: a planet passes between the star and Earth once in each of its 4.0-day orbits.
a clump of dust orbits the star and blocks its light.
a cool, dark spot on the spinning star turns into view once per rotation.
the star shrinks and swells every 4.0 days.

why.A: That is Scientist 1’s explanation.
why.B: That is Scientist 3’s explanation.
why.C: Correct — Scientist 2 ties the 4-day spacing to the star’s own spin, carrying a spot into view once each turn.
why.D: None of the scientists proposes that the star changes size.

context: Scientists 2 and 3 would both predict that the dips are:

choices.text: deeper through a blue filter than through a red one.
equally deep through every filter, blue to infrared.
caused by a body that orbits the star.

why.A: Correct — Scientist 2 says a cool spot removes more blue light, and Scientist 3 says fine dust scatters blue light more strongly.
why.B: That is Scientist 1’s prediction for a dark planet.
why.C: Scientist 2’s spot sits on the star’s surface and does not orbit it.
why.D: Scientist 1 alone predicts a flat bottom; Scientist 3 expects a slow recovery instead.

context: According to Figure 1, for about how long did the brightness stay at its lowest level?

why.A: Correct — the line sits flat at 99.0% from hour 2 to hour 6.
why.B: That is roughly the time taken to fall from normal to the lowest level, not the time spent there.
why.C: That runs from the start of the fall at hour 1 to the end of the rise at hour 7, and includes the sloping parts.
why.D: That is the whole span of the graph, most of it at normal brightness.

context: Kelm-7 has a radius of about 700,000 km. Using Scientist 1’s relationship and a dip depth of 1.0%, the planet’s radius would be about:

why.A: That multiplies the star’s radius by 0.010, treating the depth as the ratio of radii rather than its square.
why.B: That halves the correct value, as though the relationship gave a diameter rather than a radius.
why.C: That squares 0.70 rather than taking the square root of 0.010.
why.D: Correct — the ratio of radii squared is 0.010, so the ratio is 0.10, and 0.10 × 700,000 km is 70,000 km.

context: The results in Table 1 are most difficult to reconcile with which scientist’s account?

choices.text: Scientist 1’s alone, because a planet should block more blue light than red.
Scientist 3’s alone, because dust should block infrared light most strongly.
Scientists 2 and 3, because both predict deeper dips in blue light.
None of them, because no scientist says anything about colour.

why.A: Scientist 1 predicts the same depth in every colour, which is what Table 1 shows.
why.B: Scientist 3 says dust scatters blue light more strongly, not infrared.
why.C: Correct — the depth is 1.0% at 450 nm and at 900 nm alike, while both a cool spot and fine dust should dim blue light more.
why.D: All three scientists make a prediction about how the depth depends on colour.

context: Which new finding would most strengthen Scientist 2’s account?

choices.text: The dips arrived on schedule, to within two minutes, for five further years.
The depth of the dips drifted from 1.0% to 0.6% over two years.
A new measurement gave the star a spin period of 9 days.
The star’s infrared excess was confirmed at twice the earlier level.

why.A: Clockwork timing suits an orbit, and Scientist 1 cites exactly this regularity.
why.B: Correct — Scientist 2 expects spots to grow and fade over months, so a slowly changing depth is what that account predicts.
why.C: A 9-day spin would not carry a spot into view every 4.0 days, which undercuts Scientist 2.
why.D: Extra warm dust is Scientist 3’s evidence, not Scientist 2’s.

context: If Scientist 1 is correct, the 4.0-day spacing of the dips is the time the planet takes to:

choices.text: spin once completely on its own axis.
cross the face of the star from edge to edge.
send its light across the distance to Earth.

why.A: A planet’s spin does not change how much starlight it blocks, so it cannot set the spacing of the dips.
why.B: Crossing the star takes only the five hours or so of each dip.
why.C: Correct — the planet returns to the same point between star and Earth once per orbit, so the dips repeat at the orbital period.
why.D: Light travel time does not repeat and has nothing to do with the spacing of the dips.

context: According to Figure 1, the net oxygen release of the shade leaf at a light intensity of 400 µmol photons/m²/s was about:

why.A: That is the Table 1 result for 3.0 m/s from the greater height of 0.80 m.
why.B: Correct — Table 2 gives a fall time of 0.303 s from 0.45 m, and 3.0 m/s × 0.303 s is about 0.91 m.

context: Table 3 shows that the ball’s mass did not change the distance travelled. The best explanation is that, when air resistance is small:

choices.text: heavier balls fall faster but move more slowly across, and the two effects cancel.
gravity pulls harder on lighter balls, so they catch up.
heavier balls roll off the table more slowly.
all objects fall with the same acceleration.

why.A: Heavier balls do not fall faster, and every ball left the table at the same 2.0 m/s.
why.B: Gravity pulls harder on heavier balls, not lighter ones.
why.C: The launch speed was set to 2.0 m/s for every ball.

context: A falling object gains downward speed at 9.8 m/s². This means its downward speed increases by:

choices.text: 9.8 metres during each second of the fall.
9.8 m/s during each second of the fall.

why.D: That turns the unit upside down and describes no speed at all.

context: According to Figure 1, how long did an S wave take to reach a station 300 km from the earthquake?

why.A: That is the P wave at 300 km.
why.B: That is the gap between the two waves at 300 km, not the S-wave travel time.
why.C: Correct — the S-wave line reads about 86 s at 300 km.
why.D: That is the S wave at 400 km.

why.A: Correct — the P wave covers 300 km in about 50 s, and 300 ÷ 50 is 6.0.
why.B: That is the speed of the S waves, which take about 86 s for 300 km.
why.C: That divides the time by the distance, which gives seconds per kilometre.

choices.text: stays the same at every distance.
shrinks as the S wave catches up.

why.B: That is the S-wave travel time alone.
why.C: That is the P-wave travel time alone.

context: S waves cannot travel through liquid, and Earth’s outer core is liquid. A station on the opposite side of Earth from a large earthquake should therefore record:

choices.text: S waves but no P waves.
P waves but no S waves that have come straight through the core.
both kinds of wave, with the S wave arriving ahead of the P wave.

why.A: It is S waves, not P waves, that a liquid stops.
why.B: Correct — P waves can cross the liquid outer core, but S waves are stopped by it.
why.C: S waves never arrive before P waves, and a direct S wave cannot cross the core.
why.D: P waves pass through liquid as well as solid, so they still reach the far side.

context: A P-wave speed of 6.0 km/s, expressed in metres per second, is:

why.A: That multiplies by 10 instead of 1000.
why.B: That multiplies by 100 instead of 1000.
why.C: That divides by 1000 when it should multiply.

context: According to Scientist 3, large size benefits lizards on Tarra because a large lizard:

choices.text: stays warm for longer after basking.
is harder for predatory birds to catch.
wins fights over food and basking sites.
needs less food than a small lizard.

why.A: Correct — Scientist 3 says a large body loses warmth more slowly, keeping the lizard active longer on cool days.
why.B: Scientist 1 discusses birds, and says large lizards are easier to spot, not harder to catch.
why.C: That is Scientist 2’s argument about crowding.
why.D: None of the scientists claims that a larger lizard needs less food.

context: Unlike Scientist 1, Scientist 2 considers the scarcity of predatory birds on Tarra important mainly because it has:

choices.text: let each lizard live long enough to keep on growing throughout its life.
allowed lizard numbers to rise until lizards compete with one another.
kept the island cooler than the mainland.
left more beetles for each lizard.

why.A: That is Scientist 1’s reason for thinking the lack of predators matters.
why.B: Correct — Scientist 2 says fewer predators let the population reach high density, and competition at that density favours large lizards.
why.C: Predators have no bearing on the island’s temperature in any account.
why.D: Scientist 2 argues the reverse: crowding means lizards compete for food.

context: According to Table 1, the mean adult mass of lizards on Tarra is about how many times the mainland mean?

why.A: That divides the mainland mass by the Tarra mass, the ratio turned upside down.
why.B: That is the difference in grams, 58 − 21, not a ratio.
why.C: That is the ratio of lizard densities, not of masses.
why.D: Correct — 58 g ÷ 21 g is about 2.8.

context: One hectare is 10,000 m². Based on Table 1, the beetle prey available per lizard on Tarra is about what fraction of that available per lizard on the mainland?

why.A: Prey per square metre is nearly the same, but Tarra has far more lizards sharing it.
why.B: That compares prey per square metre, 1.3 against 1.2, and ignores the number of lizards.
why.C: Correct — per lizard the mainland has 1.2 × 10,000 ÷ 40, or 300 g, and Tarra 1.3 × 10,000 ÷ 310, or about 42 g.
why.D: That inverts the ratio; crowding leaves each Tarra lizard with less prey, not more.

context: A second island, Olm, has 0.4 predatory birds per km², a mean July temperature of 25 °C, and lizards of the same species averaging 55 g. This finding would most weaken the account of:

why.A: Few predators and large lizards on Olm is the pairing Scientist 1 predicts.
why.B: Olm’s lizard density is not given, so the finding neither supports nor undercuts crowding.
why.C: Correct — Olm is warmer than the mainland yet its lizards are large, which a cooling-driven account cannot explain.
why.D: The finding fits Scientist 1, says nothing about Scientist 2, and cuts against Scientist 3 alone.

context: Lizards are ectotherms. This means that a lizard:

choices.text: keeps its body at a constant temperature using heat from its food.
warms its body mainly with heat from its surroundings.
cannot survive for any length of time in air colder than 19 °C.

why.A: That describes an endotherm, such as a bird or a mammal.
why.B: Correct — an ectotherm depends on outside sources such as sunshine, which is why basking matters in Scientist 3’s account.
why.C: Ectotherms survive cool air by becoming less active; there is no such fixed limit.
why.D: Shivering to make heat is typical of endotherms.

context: According to Table 2, the freezing point of the 0.50 mol/kg sucrose solution was:

why.A: That is sodium chloride at 0.50 mol/kg, in Table 1.
why.B: Correct — Table 2 pairs 0.50 mol/kg with a freezing point of −0.94 °C.
why.C: That is sucrose at 0.20 mol/kg.
why.D: That is sucrose at 1.00 mol/kg.

context: Including sucrose alongside the two salts allowed the student to:

choices.text: compare a solute that separates into ions with one that does not.
measure how quickly each solution froze.
test whether pure water freezes at 0.00 °C.
use a larger mass of water than in the other experiments.

why.A: Correct — sucrose dissolves as whole molecules, while NaCl and CaCl₂ split into ions, so their results can be set side by side.
why.B: Only the temperature at which ice appeared was recorded, not how long freezing took.
why.C: The freezing point of pure water is given in the passage rather than tested.
why.D: Every solution was made with the same 1.00 kg of water.

context: A student hypothesizes that equal concentrations of any two solutes lower the freezing point by equal amounts. Do Tables 1 and 2 support this?

choices.text: Yes, because both freezing points fall as concentration rises.
Yes, because both kinds of solution freeze below 0.00 °C at every concentration tested.

why.D: Potato cells do not grow measurably in 24 hours, and oxygen could not account for a 14% gain.

context: The voltage reverses direction between the entering pulse and the leaving pulse. The best explanation is that:

choices.text: the magnet turns end over end as it falls through the coil.
the coil’s resistance reverses direction while the magnet is inside it.

context: A geologist finds a rock in which large crystals, several millimetres long, are scattered through a mass of crystals too small to see. Based on the passage, the most likely history of this rock is that it:

choices.text: cooled rapidly in water from the start, as obsidian did.
cooled slowly at depth, then quickly after it erupted at the surface.
cooled quickly at the surface first and then slowly deep underground.
cooled at one steady rate from start to finish.

context: According to Student 1, heat is:

context: According to Scientist 2, stripes help zebras by:

Zebras graze for longer at midday than other grazing animals do.

context: Scientist 2 says black stripes grow hotter than white ones in the sun. This is because black surfaces:

choices.text: are always thicker than white ones.

why.B: Correct — a black surface absorbs most visible light, while a white one reflects most of it.

context: According to Student 3, the candle goes out because:

context: According to Figure 1, how old is the crust 600 km from Ridge B?

context: The tidal range is largest at new moon and full moon because at those times:

why.D: Two high tides take 24.8 h, a little more than a day, so their clock times drift.

context: The star in Figure 1 appears to dim during a transit mainly because Planet b:

pulls on the star, which shrinks the star’s surface.

context: Scientists describe the link between sea ice and sunlight as a feedback that speeds up melting. Based on Table 1, which sequence best explains this feedback?

why.B: Fresh snow has the highest albedo in Table 1, so it raises the ice’s albedo and reduces absorption.
why.C: A melt pond’s albedo, 0.25, is lower than bare ice’s 0.60, so ponds lower the albedo and warm the ice.

context: A scientist hypothesizes that when melt ponds form on bare sea ice, the surface absorbs more sunlight. Do the data in Table 1 support this hypothesis?

choices.text: No; a melt pond absorbs less sunlight than open ocean does.
No; a melt pond absorbs 225 W/m² and bare ice absorbs 282 W/m².
Yes; a melt pond absorbs nearly twice as much.

why.A: The hypothesis compares melt ponds with bare ice, not with open ocean.
why.B: Bare ice absorbs 120 W/m²; 282 W/m² is the figure for open ocean.
why.C: Correct — a melt pond absorbs 225 W/m² and bare ice only 120 W/m², so the same 300 W/m² of sunlight puts nearly twice as much energy into a melt pond as into bare ice.
why.D: A melt pond’s albedo, 0.25, is lower than bare ice’s 0.60, which is why it absorbs more.

context: According to Figure 1, what is the peak wavelength of a star with a surface temperature of 6000 K?

context: Which variable was deliberately changed in Experiment 2?

context: According to Scientist 1, leaves turn yellow in autumn because:

the tree makes new yellow pigment to shield the leaf from sunlight.

context: Based on Table 1, the amount of chlorophyll in the leaves on October 8 was most likely about:

why.A: That lies between the September 15 and October 1 values, earlier than October 8.

choices.text: absorbs red and blue light and reflects the green light.

context: According to Scientist 2, the Sun’s energy comes from:

heat left over from when it first formed.
its material sinking inward as the Sun shrinks.
its material burning, as coal burns in air.

context: Scientist 3 says fusion happens only in the extremely hot core. Hydrogen nuclei fuse only at such high temperatures because:

why.B: Hydrogen nuclei are positively charged protons, and nuclei do not melt.
